Mr. Speaker, I do not propose, at this moment, to offer any opposition to the second reading of the Bill ; but I desire to intimate to the mover that at some subsequent day I shall move an amendment to the Bill which 1 think will possibly meet with the approbation of this House. To my mind, we are going too far in the incorporation of new banks. It strikes me that, as during the present session, we have granted some six new charters, besides two others on the list, possibly it is time to call a halt. There is a feeling throughout the country that our banks, in order to obtain profitable business have taken too many investments outside of this country, and it is a question whether we are right in allowing our banking institutions to stretch out into the United States too far, to invest in American securities and encourage by their doing so, the practice of speculation which is rife in this country, and which has caused such very material losses to our people. I do not charge the banks, in the first place, with anything of that kind ; but I do say that without the chartered banks these speculations cannot be carried on, and if we wish to strike a blow at these speculative operations that have caused so much loss, injury, suffering and sorrow to the people of this country during the present year, we must go back to the source of this trouble. If we can minimize it in any way, I think it is the duty of parliament to deal with the question. The purport of my amendment is to limit the investments of banks so that they will not be
able to assist brokers, loan companies and others who are engaged in this speculative business in obtaining the requisite money to carry on these operations. I believe that if we minimize the advances along that line, we shall minimize the injurious consequences of the investment of large amounts of money on call loans in the United States on American stocks. I will simply read the amendment I have to propose, so that the promoter may understand the position, and, having stated the course I intend to pursue. I shall allow the Bill, so far as I am concerned, to go to the Committee on Banking and Commerce where the matter can be dealt with. I am reminded by a question from the hon. member from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) to say that I have u >
particular desire to interfere with the charter of this bank any more than that of any other. This is not a special matter in the case of this bank at all. The amendment 1 shall propose is as follows :
Notwithstanding anything contained in the Bank Act, the said bank shall not, either directly or indirectly, lend money or make advances upon the security of, or take as collateral security for any loan made by it, the bonds, stocks and other securities or obligations of any company or corporation or body corporate not incorporated by the parliament of Great Britain, or by the parliament of Canada or of a province of Canada, until the consent thereto by the shareholders of said bank shall have been obtained at a special meeting of the said bank specially called for that purpose.
Or I may propose the amendment without the latter clause.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I would think it would be a very proper time for the hon. minister to give us some statement of the general policy of the government in regard to transportation west of Lake Superior and indeed from that to the Atlantic coast. We have asked that information in this House from time to time, but I do not think we have gathered very much thus far, except possibly the individual views of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals expressed outside of the House. We have not only this measure but another very important measure before the House at this time a measure which, as we supposed, was coming up for consideration this afternoon-I refer to the Bill to incorporate the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company-and in the meantime, from influential organs of public opinion which are supposed to be largely in the confidence of the government, we are receiving intimations that the government is likely to propose a policy in regard to the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to some point farther west. It seems to me that in considering the aid which we shall grant to so important a part of the transportation system of Canada as this road will undoubtedly be, it would be

useful to the House-indeed it is due to the House-to have some statement from the government, or from the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, as to what the policy of the government is in regard to the whole scheme of transportation and particularly in regard to transcontinental railways. It is asking the House to take something of a leap in the dark when we are desired to deal with this Bill without any information such as that which I have suggested. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals said, when the resolutions were being discussed in committee, that this line of some 720 miles in length which we are now being asked to assist would stand by itself separate and apart from any general scheme of transportation. I am inclined to take issue very strongly with the hon. minister in regard to that. I do not think this line should stand by itself. This is a very important line indeed; We have a system shown on the plan or on the map which the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has laid on the Table to-day, and we see that this proposed system will extend very far indeed towards the Pacific coast. We know that, if not the same company, at all events the same gentlemen have obtained a charter to the Pacific coast, and it has been publicly announced on their behalf that their intention is eventually to extend their line to the Pacific coast and to own and control a transcontinental line. Well, it becomes very important indeed that the government should, at this stage, give the House its policy in regard to the whole system of transportation. Has the government made up its mind, or if not, when does it expect to make up its mind, as to whether or not it will leave this question of transcontinental railways entirely in the hands of private individuals or companies granting them for that purpose such assistance as may be thought reasonable ? Has the government under consideration the question of extending the Intercolonial Railway to any point farther west ? I do not think that I am asking too much of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals when I ask him to give the views of the government to the House in regard to that very important question at this stage. As I said before I do not think there is any more proper time for doing so than on this occasion when we are asked to deal by way of very substantial assistance with a line which must become part of a transcontinental system sooner or later.
_ The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS. Mr. Chairman, I do not blame my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) for making the request for information which he has made to the government in respect of the general question of transportation, but in doing so I do not admit that he would have been perfectly entitled to make Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
such a request though this proposition were not under the consideration of the committee. I cannot help regarding the question of aid to the Canadian Northern as a question which is not at all necessarily or otherwise connected with the matter with respect to which the hon. gentleman desires us to give him further knowledge. The hon. member of course is aware that proposals have been made to the government respecting the construction of another transcontinental line. If we cannot so describe the line of the Canadian Northern, at all events, there is one transcontinental line which will justify me in speaking of the proposals which are before the government as proposals respecting another transcontinental line. The present line of the Canadian Northern is one which was not projected, and which has not been aided from the standpoint of a line from the Pacific to the Atlantic. We have never had from the gentlemen who are interested in the Canadian Northern any request that they should be regarded as having in contemplating a line reaching from the Atlantic ocean at an early date, or as part of any scheme or plan which they say are to carx-y out in the immediate future. They came before the government a year ago and my hon. friend knows what transpired just before the session came to a close, when the right hon. Premier (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) stated that the government had a very important proposal before them. I do not know whether he referred to the Canadian Northern by name, but it was in reference to the Canadian Northern that he spoke. They were very anxious to get into the country which their charter authorized them to traverse, and the government were very anxious that they should do so, for the reasons that that country was beginning to fill up and is being looked to by new settlers as a very desirable country in which to settle and we felt that for the encouragement of settlement by people who had not gone through, and for the further encouragement of people who had gone through, it was essential that the line of the Canadian Northern by the route, plans of which had been submitted to the government and subsequently approved, should be constructed and that these gentlemen should at the earliest possible day enter upon the prosecution of their work.
We are urging the matter now because we feel that it is only fair to that company and it is only fair to the enterprise itself that it should be known parliament had given its sanction, so that they would be in a position to finance the project without any further delay. We regard it as vitally important that this road should be built with all possible speed, and to that end it is our purpose and intention to facilitate it, in every way in our power, of course, with the sanction and approval of parlia-

ment. That proposition therefore was one with which the government practically dealt with so far as the government could deal with it until parliament had passed its approval upon their proposals; and the government dealt with it before any question had come before us or had been submitted to us from any quarter by any other organization looking to the construction of a line from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Therefore this proposition which is before us to-day is in fact a separate and distinct proposition from the other. No one imagines for a moment that the building of this Canadian Northern line will exhaust the territory which we have available for settlement in our prairie region; no one will imagine for a moment that another line-if it shall be incorporated by parliament, and built, pursuing a more northerly route some miles distant from the most northerly line now located-no one will imagine for a moment that it will not go through a country which will be productive from every point of view. And as that line will likely, when it is taken up by the government, reach the Pacific and reach it as speedily ns possible, and will be an all Canadian route when it is constructed ; it is a separate and totally distinct proposition from that with which we have now to deal, and it is a proposition that is not in the slightest degree affected, as it appears to me, by the proposals which are now under the consideration of the committee.
I would be very glad indeed to inform my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) what decision the government had arrived at in respect to another transcontinental line, but when the submission is made to parliament by the government that submission must be a precise one; it must be a definite one; it must be one made with some detail; it must be one which has been well considered, and it would be premature, entirely premature, until all these various considerations have been passed on by the government and have been decided upon, that any statement should be made to parliament. I can say to my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) that we are as anxious as he is to be in a jiosition to announce to parliament whether we are going to ask parliament to take up the question of another transcontinental line at this session, or are going to defer it to a later period. Any member of the government would be as glad as my hon. friend, when a decision is reached, to present all the details which may bear upon so large a problem as that. We are just as keen as he is to reach a decision upon these matters. But that decision has not yet been reached and it would be impossible to make any announcement to parliament upon the subject now. I do not think that very many days will elapse before we will be able to take parliament fully into our confidence upon the subject, but in the meantime my hon. friend will have to rest content with the assurance, that the reason why the government is not giving him any more information to-day is not because we have information which we could give him and which we are withholding, but because we have not reached that point which we think it necessary to reach in order that we may put before the House and before the country, propositions which are well considered, which are practical, which are precise, which are definite, and which are such as we feel we can defend.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
The Minister of Railways has told us explicitly that the government has not yet come to a decision in reference to the Grand Trunk transcontinental railway. As my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) has pointed out, the Canadian Northern Railway people have announced that they intend not only to build to Edmonton but to reach the Pacific coast. In fact they shortened their route in order to make it available as the shortest possible transcontinental line. They also abandoned that portion of the I-Iudson Bay Railway and their western extension for the purpose of starting afresh at a point which would give them the shortest connection between Winnipeg and Edmonton. It is a well known fact that it is their intention to go to the coast. The government have these facts before them, and we have had the statement of the Prime Minister that he does not intend to subsidize a second transcontinental road across the continent. All this being so, the government must have considered how far they intend to go with the Grand Trunk Railway Pacific in their proposal to build a road across the continent. The hon. minister says that it may be the intention of the government to assist a road north of the proposed Canadian Northern Railway road which runs to Edmonton and thence to the coast. He says there is plenty of room in that country for another railway. Of course there is. But what the leader of the oj>po-sition wants to know is : did not the government consider all these things when they came to a decision to assist the Canadian Northern Railway 1 The government must have considered that. What would be the use of the Grand Trunk Railway or any other railway built by a private company from Quebec, to end in Winnipeg. It would not be worth anything to any company unless it had a western connection and a connection with the great lakes also. When they get to Winnipeg they must have connection with the fertile plains west and also with Lake Superior, and also, as I believe, in the near future, with the Hudson Bay, whence the wheat of that section of the country will be shipped to the markets of the world. All that must have been considered by the government when they came to a decision to assist the Canadian Northern Railway to Edmonton. Is this to be a road merely for the purpose of carrying immigrants and for taking out the grain

from that section of the country. Not at all. The assistance that is given to the Canadian Northern Railway must be in the light of its being a transcontinental road and before the government assisted it they must have come to a conclusion as to whether they were going to assist two roads to the Pacific coast or not. I should judge, from the statement of the hon. Minister of Railways, that the government have not come to a conclusion upon the subject-that they have not been able to make an arrangement between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern. After the statement of the premier, they would not come to the House and ask for a subsidy for another transcontinental railway ; because it is well known that the Canadian Northern Railway intend building to the Pacific coast. That company is being assisted by this government to the extent of ,$13,000 per mile, not for the purpose merely of reaching Edmonton. Their ulterior object, as every man in this country knows, is to construct a transcontinental road. Therefore, I argue that the whole subject must have been well considered by the government, they must have come to some conclusion in reference to it, find they ought to be prepared to take the House into their confidence and state whether, in the event of the Canadian Northern Railway Company projecting their line to the Pacific coast, it is their intention to assist the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway from Quebec to Winnipeg. As I have said before, unless the Grand Trunk Railway Company have the right to build to the Pacific coast, and to extend colonization lines into different parts of the country, a line from Quebec to Winnipeg would be an entirely useless one. In view of the statement of the premier, the application of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and the intention of the Canadian Northern Railway Company to build to the Pacific coast, surely the House and the country are entitled to more information than has been given by the Minister of Railways on this important subject.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I think the House is entitled to more information on this subject than has been given on many occasions. The hon. Minister of Railways says that the reason this Canadian Northern Railway system has never been treated as a transcontinental system is that its promoters have never informed the government that they had the ambition to build a transcontinental railway. It has been rumoured for more than a year past, to my knowledge, that they were ambitious to build through to the Pacific coast. When the lines which are now under construction are completed, for which the government are prepared to guarantee the interest, the Canadian Northern Railway Company will have an independent system by which they will be able to reach Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
the head waters of the lakes, and ship the products of the country to the markets of the world. In a sense, when they reach the head of the lakes, they reach tlie seaboard almost as much as would a railroad built from Winnipeg to Quebec, the only difference being that they reach fresh water instead of salt water; for the ports at the head of tlie lakes are open almost as many months of the year as the port of Quebec. To my mind it is ridiculous to say that the Canadian Northern Railway has not been considered in the light of a transcontinental railway. Can the government justify, before this House and the country, the bonus-ing of another railway paralleling the Canadian Northern Railway beyond Winnipeg V Are they of opinion that, with the Canadian Pacific Railway and its branches, and with the Canadian Northern Railway and its branches, there will be sufficient railway facilities in the north-west for some time to come 1 Then, what will be the object of building a line from Quebec to Winnipeg ? These are subjects which the government must have considered, and on which they ought to be able to give us some preliminary facts and figures. For my part, I feel that the time has arrived when the government should be in a position to say more to the House than they have said on the transportation question.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I want to refer to one statement the Minister of Railways made. He said it is premature to give the statement to the House. Well, this House has been sitting for over three months and a half, and we must be drawing within measurable distance of the end of the session ; surely the House ought to be in possession of the information soon, or otherwise not be expected to consider the subject during the present session. If the government cannot give the information now and yet purpose maturing their plans before this House is prorogued, then they must come down in the dying hours of the session with their decision, just as we have had resolutions regarding railways many times in the past. I think that is hardly fair to the House. In this instance the information is doubly important, because it has reference to a great through railway that ought to be considered as a whole, and not in piecemeal, as it is by these resolutions. We have had various rumours in the press of late, one being that the government have decided to build a line from Quebec to Winnipeg as a government line. If that be the case, I respectfully submit that the House and the country ought to know it. It has also been rumoured that the government have reached no conclusion, but that there is a diversity of opinion amongst the members of the cabinet on the subject. If that be so, let them state that they cannot reach a conclusion this session, and will not be prepared to submit any proposition to

the House during the present session ; and then they can go on and mature their plans. But it is due to the House and the country that we should have some information on the subject one way or the other at this stage of this session, so that we may know what is before us for the balance of the session.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I rise, Mr. Chairman, to emphasize the position taken by lion, gentlemen on this side of the House. It seems to me that it is the most reasonable proposition that could emanate from the opposition, to ask the hon. gentleman and his colleagues wliat they propose to do with regard to providing additional facilities for the solution of the transportation problem by giving aid for the construction of additional lines. The hon. Minister of Railways has said that the Mackenzie & Mann outfit was never looked upon as a transcontinental line.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I did not say that. What I said was that they had never approached the government from that point of view at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
Of course, it would be an insult to the intelligence of the hon. minister to think, for one moment, that he was not fully aware of the efforts this company has been making during the past few years to improve its position, and the ultimate object which it has in view and which it hopes to attain by the legislation it has secured in this House for the promotion of the different sections of its line. He must be aware that when the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway scheme was first mooted, when notice was first given of the intention of its promoters to apply for incorporation, its eastern terminus was at Gravenhurst. Since then the Mackenzie & Mann Company have practically gained control of the Great Northern Railway, which gives them a line from Quebec to Montreal, and eventually to Ottawa ; and he also knows that they have charters which will extend their system from their present terminus to the Pacific coast. He must also be aware of the fact that in Ontario, they are making connection between their present terminus at Port Arthur with Sudbury, and finally Toronto. If such a scheme cannot be considered transcontinental, I would like to ask how the hon. minister can look upon the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway as a transcontinental scheme ? That scheme had first its eastern terminus at Gravenhurst, but by degrees it has extended it east to Montreal and then to Quebec and now down to Moncton. What claim has this new proposition to be considered transcontinental that is not possessed by that of Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann ? In my humble judgment these gentlemen have proved themselves practical railway builders, and their enterprise is certainly entitled to be considered as transcontinental
in its character. If that be the case, we should have a fuller explanation of the policy of the government than has been vouchsafed by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. Does the hon. minister seriously think that the construction of a line from Quebec to Winnipeg will aid very materially in the solution of the transportation problem ? Would it not be wise for the government to make up their minds and put the opposition in possession of the conclusions they come to with regard to the solution of this problem before asking us to consent to a government guarantee or bonus, amounting to millions of dollars, in order to aid tlie construction of the Mackenzie & Mann lines ? The policy that ought to be adopted is the one that will at the earliest moment open up the prairie lands of the North-west; and as a complement of that policy are the additional facilities that should be provided at Port Arthur and Fort William and the harbours on tlie eastern side of Georgian bay. It is absurd to say that we are going to solve the problem of furnishing sufficient transportation facilities, if we content ourselves with guaranteeing the bonds or bonusing a road whose eastern terminus will be at Quebec and its western at Winnipeg. The construction of such a line is not necessary. We have the Intercolonial Railway running from Quebec to Montreal, which can be extended as far west as the government choose to take it. We have also the transcontinental line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and we have tlie Grand Trunk Railway running from Quebec westward to North Bay. Why should not the government devise some plan for making use of tlie road already constructed north of Lake Superior, where the traffic is now very light ? Why not make an agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway which would secure running rights over that section for the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canada Atlantic Railway, and if necessary, the Intercolonial Railway, so that these roads might get up to tlie North-west, while the Canadian Northern Railway system could at tlie same time come from Port Arthur eastward ? A proposition of that kind would meet the approval of the House, and the opposition have a right to complain of the meagreness of the information supplied by the government as to what the intention of the government really is.
I have noticed in the Toronto papers that an attempt is being made to promote tlie construction and operation by the government of a road between Quebec and Winnipeg. Will the hon. gentleman vouchsafe any information on that subject ? Is it tlie intention of the government to shelve the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme for this session, so far as giving any aid to it is concerned, or to construct a national road from Quebec to Winnipeg and operate it ?

We have had the most meagre information on these points, and it is only right that we should be furnished with such information as I have suggested before we proceed further with the consideration of this Bill.
Another point I would lay before the hon. minister is this : Provision is made further on in this Bill that the Mackenzie & Mann enterprise shall not be consolidated witli the Canadian Pacific Railway, that its proprietors shall not sell it out to the Canadian Pacific Railway, or pass it under the control of that company. Why is there a provision made to prevent the absorption of the Mackenzie & Mann system by the Canadian Pacific Railway ? Why is not a similar provision inserted respecting its absorption by the Grand Trunk Pacific or any other transcontinental line that may be constructed ? It certainly seems to me that we have not the information we have a right to expect, and I strongly support the position taken by my hon. leader, namely, that tlie government should give us more information than they have yet vouchsafed before asking us to proceed further with so important a measure. We ought certainly to have a more definite declaration from the government as to what their transportation schemes really are and how they hope to give the country a satisfactory solution of that most pressing problem now waiting to be solved. The way these schemes are presented to us is not at all satisfactory, and we have the right to expect better things of a government which claims to be before everything else a business administration. I hope that the government will give us additional information or tell us that they have no policy to lay before the House, and that the best thing they can give us is this proposition to aid the Mackenzie & Mann project in the Northwest.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I have nothing to add to the statement I have already made to the committee. I stated in effect that the government had not matured its plans sufficiently to lay them before parliament. In that respect we lay ourselves open to any reflection which the hon. gentleman may choose to cast upon us, but not having matured our plans, it is a physical and moral impossibility for me to present them to the House. I hope my hon. friend now understands why I do not give him information tie asks.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I thank the hon. gentleman for this information. He is perfectly candid and frank, and I would ask him, in view of the statement he has just made, whether it would not be more reasonable to postpone further consideration of the Bill before us until the government have made up their minds and laid before parliament a completed scheme ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I think not, and I will -tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) why. It is for the very reason that he himself stated to this committee-the absolute necessity of providing railway facilities for the people who are already living in the district to be traversed by the road and who are now going there. We want to afford these facilities at the earliest possible moment; we are under engagement to do it, and we are carrying out that engagement, so far as lies in our power, by asking parliament for the authority provided in this Bill. Whether there is any transcontinental railway determined upon so far as government action is concerned, or whether it is not, is not material, so far as the present proposal is concerned, in my opinion. I think this road should go forward with all possible despatch. I think that every day of delay counts, because I am sure the gentlemen who are concerned in this undertaking will require to finance it, and should have an opportunity to do so at a season when financial arrangements can be made. We should not be justified in delaying to ask parliament to take action until we had matured our plans with regard to other matters that may be before us.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
We all remember very well that this project was before the House, or at least before the government, last session; and, if it is to be regarded in the light in which the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) presents it to the House to-day, I should think the government should not care about mentioning the word ' delay ' in connection with it. I understood, certainly, from what took place at the end of last session, and from the comments which were made by the government press at the close of the session, that the government delayed doing last session what they are doing now for the very reason that this was a transcontinental scheme, and they proposed to have a policy with regard to it. If it is not to be regarded in .the light in which it is presented on this side of the House, why has there been delay for more than, a year in giving these railway facilities to the North-west Territories ? Why did not the government bring down .the proposition more than a year ago ? Why is it that now they present it to the House and still have no policy, though the question of policy must have been under consideration for a year at least ? Now, the government is face to face with one of two positions with regard to this matter. Either they did regard this line, a year ago, ns of so much importance in connection with the question of transcontinental transportation that they deemed it wise to do nothing until they could have a definite and specific policy with regard to that great question-they apparently did take that view of it a year ago, and therefore held their hands-or, on the other

hand, if they did not take that view a year ago, as I have said, there seemed to have been no good reason why there was a waste of at least a year in providing any facilities for this very important section of the Northwest Territories at a time, when, as the government knew, immigration was pouring in at a rapid rate, and was likely to increase in proportion during the present year. It seems to me that the delay that has taken place during the past year can only be because the government regarded it in the light in which we, on this side regard it now. What justification then, have the government to come down, three and a half months after the beginning of the present session, still telling parliament they have not matured a policy with regard to this great question ? I, for one, shall object strenuously to having a great question like this dealt with by parliament during the last ten days or fortnight of the session. As this is a matter which, in some shape or other, has been under consideration for at least a year, it would be treating, not only parliament but the country, unfairly, to ask that the people's representatives should consider it hurriedly, as such matters have to be considered in the closing days of a session. And I say that if the government are not prepared to deal with this question from the standpoint of a definite and specific policy of transcontinental railway connection, they ought to be so prepared, having had the question under consideration for at least a year. And, when the hon. gentleman speaks, as he does, of this line, comprising about seven hundred and thirty miles of railway, as! standing alone, standing by itself, something to be dealt with apart from the great general question, I do not agree with him. I believe that the people of the North-west now look, or at least they will in the future look, to the question of communication with the Pacific coast as of very great importance to them- perhaps as of as great importance to them as the question of transportation to the Atlantic coast. If our opportunities with regard to trade on the Pacific ocean and with the countries beyond the Pacific ocean are to any extent realized, it will be just as important to the constituents of my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) that there should be means of communication, and good means of communication, from that portion of the country to the Pacific, as that there should be means of transportation to the Atlantic. I do not say it is of such importance now, but I say it is very likely to be of as much importance in the future. And, even at the present, it is of importance that that portion of the country should have the means of communication with the great province of British Columbia. For these reasons, I must dissent, notwithstanding the arguments of the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair), from the position which he has taken in saying that this 600 miles of rail-176
way from Gilbert Plains to Edmonton can be regarded as standing by itself and not necessarily connected with a great scheme of transcontinental transportation.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The Minister of Railways and Canals provides in this Bill, section S, th#t it shall be unlawful for the Canadian Northern Railway to lease or sell any of its lines or any portion thereof to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Now, as we are aware, the Canadian Northern goes through the State of Minnesota, having a length in that state of about one hundred miles. If it is to be unlawful for the Canadian Northern Railway Company to amalgamate with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, a Canadian corporation, would it not be wise to make it unlawful also for them to amalgamate with an American corporation ? There have been efforts in the past, and there are efforts to-day, to divert our trade to American channels. It seems to me that it would be the part of wisdom for the government to say that the Canadian Northern shall not amalgamate with any American corporation that would divert our trade to American ports. That would be the easiest thing in the world. Any one who knows that part of the country will see, I hope, thei strength of the position I take. I fully recognize, with the hon. minister, that it is important to give additional means of transportation to our North-west friends. But, at the same time, it seems to me that we should never lose sight of the national fact, that we must not spare any efforts, we must not spare any means, to secure for ourselves the trade that we are building up in the west. So I would be very thankful indeed if the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals were in a position to offer us some information as to the point I am now raising.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I think it must be plain that from the first moment the Canadian Northern acquired a charter from parliament authorizing it to build into the Northwestern country, the condition was annexed that they should not be allowed to amalgamate with the Canadian Pacific Railway. That was the feeling and temper of parliament at that time, and that feeling and temper were shown in the agreement that was entered into by the Canadian Northern with the Manitoba government. That stipulation is one of the clauses of that contract. It was thought well, seeing that had been the expressed desire of parliament, that it should be continued in the existing arrangement. I do not know that a clause of this sort is of much value, because it will always be open to parliament to allow the Canadian Northern to amalgamate with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and it could not make any agreement, that is to say, the company could not be amalgamated unless parliament did give them power. Whether or not



you have a clause of this kind in the present legislation or any other charter, they could not do it without. There is, however, something beyond that in the clause which says that they may not make pooling arrangements nor enter into an agreement whereby rates upon freights or passengers shall be pooled. That is in addition, and that has been thought a wise and prudent provision, and is contained I think in all other contracts and agreements that have been made by the Canadian Northern, as well with the provincial government of Manitoba as with ourselves. My hon. friend has stated that this road runs a hundred miles in the state of Minnesota. The fact is it is only about fifty miles. But why was that ? It was because it would have been necessary, when the road was being constructed, in order that it should continue through Canadian territory, to incur a very large expense to cross the lake within Canadian territory ; and it was one of the understandings at that time with the Canadian Northern when we gave them assistance to construct the Rainy river branch, that if, at any future time, it was considered desir-abie that the road should take a short cut and should be built across the Lake of the Woods, the company would, upon receiving assistance, make that change in the route. I presume they will be prepared to carry it out at any time with reasonable assistance.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
Is there an understanding of that kind with the company ?
The MINISTER Ui' RAILWAYS AND CANALS. There was an understanding of that kind. I was asked by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) why the same restriction should not apply to other companies. There are no other companies existing in that country at present, and if parliament chooses at any time to impose that restriction upon any company that is incorporated, it is quite free to do so. Whatever we might put in here, it would be necessary that legislation should be had by any other company chartered for the purpose of building through that country if it desired to make connection with the Canadian Northern.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I do not object to the clause stating that the Canadian Northern may not amalgamate with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I see the reason of that. The people of the west want competition, and they believe, rightly or wrongly, that there will be no arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern, because there is such a clause in the Bill. I hope they are right. But the point to which I wish again to call the attention of the Minister, is that if it is made unlawful for the Canadian Northern in the present Bill to amalgamate with the Canadian

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Pacific Railway, it seems to me it should be made unlawful also to amalgamate with any American corporation.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: They could not amalgamate without we gave them the power.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I think the hon. member must be aware of the fact that the traffic from our western country could not be diverted to the south and carried away by American railways without an amalgamation between an American railway and a Canadian road. It would be mere matter of shipment; and is the hon. gentleman prepared to say, is there any member of this parliament prepared to say, that we should put a clause in any charter we grant to a Canadian railway, that it should not be allowed to ship any of its products to the south of the boundary line, even though its products might be required there for consumption ? Would anybody have any reason to say that that would be wise legislation ? The only way, it strikes me, by which you could prevent the shipping of the products of the west via the United States railways to the sea, is by making it to the interest and advantage of Canadian railways to ship them otherwise.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: How can that best be done ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: By constructing the shortest possible line to the ocean over Canadian territory. My hon. friend knows further that even if you pass legislation of that kind, you cannot say that the shipper shall not have a right to send his products whichever way he pleases to reach their destination. Let my hon. friend appeal to the representatives from the west, and ask them what they would think of a clause of that kind. They would say that their people would not sustain them if they voted for any such a proposition. You have to allow trade to follow the line of least resistance in reaching its destination. You cannot by legislation do otherwise. You can only make the inducement strong enough by making the Canadian route the shortest and best.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I beg to take the strongest possible objection to the statements of my hon. friend the Minister of. Railways and Canals. This is not a question for the west or for the east. It is a Canadian question in the broad sense. The west is not the only portion of Canada that is concerned in the measure that, is before parliament to-day. The west is not voting the money alone. This country is pledging its credit to an enterprise which is a national enterprise, and it is a national question with which parliament has to deal. Again I say it is not a question for the west exclusively, and to that view I have objected every time the point has been raised. Our ambition is to establish trade between the different provinces as far as it is possible to do so. The way of doing that, as the hon. minister has stated, is to provide communication. I do not ask that it shall be forbidden that any railway corporation shall ship to the other side of the line. That would be a preposterous proposition. Nobody thinks of it. I do not suggest that, but I suggest a clause concerning American railways similar to the one which is included concerning the Canadian Pacific Railway. I would like to prevent amalgamation with any of these American railways.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: My hon. friend must see that amalgamation means a combination of two companies, not for the purposes of traffic, but as a corporate body-the amalgamation of two distinct corporate bodies into one corporate body with identical interests. What effect would that have upon shipping through the United States or anywhere else?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: What I fear is the amalgamation of this Canadian Northern with some American corporation which will divert our trade.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: We are always liable to that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
The hon. minister says we are always liable to that, but that is not
an answer, in my opinion. Parliament is called upon to give a large guarantee after having given a large amount of money to Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann. Is it not reasonable that the Canadian people should have by law the assurance that this corporation which is being helped with Canadian money be not amalgamated with an American corporation ? I think I am right in that. It is not a question of shipping. It is out of the question to ask our railways not to ship goods to the other side of the line. That is not what I mean at all. 1 mean to say that we should insert a clause concerning American railways similar to the one which we have in this Bill-clause a- concerning the Canadian Pacific Railway. I shall not insist any more upon the point now. I have raised the question. Parliament is seized of it, and it is for the House to decide.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think everybody will sympathize with the desire of the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that the trade of the west should go through Canadian channels, but I think we will all agree with the remark of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) that the only way that the trade of the west can be got to go through Canadian channels is by making Canadian channels the most advantageous channels for that trade to go through. You are not going to force 100,000,000 bushels of wheat by a route that is disadvantageous from the commercial standpoint by a clause in this Act of parliament. So far as the general question which my hon. friend has raised is concerned, I fear that he has lost sight of the history of this transaction. When the question of aid to what was called the Ontario and Rainy River Railway, or what is now the Canadian Northern Railway, from Winnipeg to Port Arthur was under consideration by the government, and later by this House, the question of these 40, 50 or 60 miles going through American territory was then considered, and the question as to whether we should compel that railway company to build across the Lake of the Woods was fully dealt with at that time. It was considered by the government, and I think also by the House at a later date, that the excessive expense which would be caused to the company by compelling them to build across the Lake of the Woods could not be justified and that the desire of the company to get down to Port Arthur, to a Canadian port, and assist in transporting the grain of the west ought to be facilitated by allowing them to go around by the cheapest and shortest route. There is nothing any more dangerous in the Canadian Northern running around 40 or 50 or 60 miles through the State of Minnesota on their way to Port Arthur than there is in the Canadian Pacific Railway running through the state of Maine to get to St. .Tohn, and

nobody has ever suggested that special legislation" should be brought in to compel the Canadian Pacific Railway not to divert any portion of its traffic as it runs through the state of Maine on its way to a Canadian port. We know that that is impracticable legislation. The real fact is that the lines which the Canadian Northern own in the province of Manitoba were originally built by the Northern Pacific Railway, and that as matters stood at that time and before the building of this line from Winnipeg to Port Arthur, the trade did go through American channels. It went by the Northern Pacific to the port of Duluth, and the government had in mind in assisting the Canadian Northern the changing of that condition of affairs, and as a result of what has been done for this railway a very considerable amount of business has been done by the Canadian Northern and enormous quantities of grain have been taken to Port Arthur which fotherwise 'would have (been shipped by way of the port of Duluth.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Would the hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) say where that grain goes now from Port Arthur ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
That is another point. That is a point which is important, but it is a point which my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) will readily admit cannot be dealt with here. That must be dealt with in another way. What I desired to point out was that the building of this railway was for the purpose of overcoming that which was taking place at that time, and which is being counteracted to a great extent by the construction of the Canadian Northern. Would my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) suppose that when the Canadian Northern, as a business corporation, is expending $1,000,000 at Port Arthur for the purpose of building up a storage system there that will enable it to handle the grain, it would destroy that investment absolutely by making some arrangement out of which it would get no financial advantage, and as a result of which its traffic would be handed over to the control of somebody else ? The proposition is preposterous. What we must do in the consideration of this whole question from beginning to end is to endeavour to make our arrangements of such a character and to improve our transportation in such a way that Canadian channels will be more advantageous than the American, and I think that the development of the Canadian Northern Railway, if it is attentively considered, will be found to be one of the most effective instruments in earying that into effect in so far as it has gone up to the present time, and instead of the product of the prairies going, to a considerable degree, by way of the Northern Pacific through American channels, as in former years, through the inauguration of this system it will go through Canadian channels. It seems to me that the objection Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
which has been raised is an artificial one, and cannot be considered to have any force or effect upon the proposition as it is now before the committee.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Kindly look at the map which is placed before us. Here is Port Arthur and here is Duluth. We are all aware that Mr. Hill's system centres at Duluth. I suppose that Duluth has the most magnificent elevators in the world. Mr. Hill owns the greatest part of them and other people own the balance. There is nothing easier than for Mr. Hill to buy the Canadian Northern and divert all the trade from the west to that port. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sifton) says that it is preposterous to suppose that Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann would destroy the fine property-and it is a fine property I am glad to say-that they have built at Port Arthur. Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann will not live for all time; men pass pretty quickly; we are not going to be so long on this side of the big ocean, and Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann will go as we all will go. We are not dealing today with men; we are dealing with the future and we are dealing with a broad situation. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has said that Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann have a charter to the Pacific ocean. So they have, and more than that they have made arrangements with the government of British Columbia to go on with their work. They are energetic men; there are no better builders of railways than these men are.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Whatever our opinion may be of their different schemes we must admit that they have shown a great deal of ability and energy.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I believe that I am not far from the mark when I say that these gentlemen intend to build their railway to the coast and they will come to us again; there is no fear as to that. They cannot build that without the credit of this parliament and they will come to this parliament. Having these facts before our eyes it seems to me that it would be the part of prudence to take our precautions. The Minister of the Interior says : You did not take such precautions when the Canadian Pacific Railway was built. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sifton) is younger than I am, and I might call his attention to the fact that most of the newspaper men in Quebec, although we were government supporters, objected very very strongly to that part of the Canadian Pacific Railway scheme. My hon. friends on the treasury benches only have to look at the debates which took place then to find that there was in the province of Quebec especially, a very strong

opposition to that part of the scheme. However, if we believe that the government of the day were not right in allowing the Canadian Pacific Railway to pass through the state of Maine, then we should not repeat that mistake. We cannot prevent the Canadian Northern Railway from passing through Minnesota; we all grant that; it is done. If an error has been made we cannot prevent it, but what I suggest-and I suggest it in a friendly way and in the interest of the country at large-what I suggest is that we shall not allow a Canadian corporation that we are all glad to help, to amalgamate with an American corporation. The Canadian North-west is developing and will develop more and more. Our national interest is to unite the different provinces by the bonds of common interests, and we are now in a position to offer the best route, provided we take means to see that our trade is not diverted from our own country. Here is a Canadian corporation which is seeking the aid and credit of this parliament, and I ask that a clause be inserted to prevent amalgamation. I do not know if this suggestion has been made before, but I believe that Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann would consent to it. However, we are not here to please corporations or contractors. Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann have not only a charter to go to the Pacific ocean but they have also a charter to the port of Quebec. When my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sifton) cited the example of the late government concerning the Canadian Pacific Railway, he lost sight of the fact that we are discussing now the possibility of pledging the credit of the country, or of giving aid to another transcontinental railway in Canadian territory exclusively. Most of the members of this House, I take it, are insisting on having an all-Canadian route, and evidently that is of importance. Those who have followed the events of the past few years will remember that In a little wrangle that took place between the Canadian Pacific Railway and my former colleague the Minister of Railways, the port of St. John was threatened with being abandoned and the port of Boston was to be adopted. If there had not been a strong public sentiment in favour of having the Canadian Pacific Railway located at a Canadian port nobody could tell what might have taken place. Railway corporations have not very big hearts; they are the properties of hundreds and thousands of people ; directors change often, and so we are not dealing with men but we are dealing with a problem and in my humble opinion that problem should be solved in the interests of Canada. It is for that reason that I urge tlie government to take into consideration the point that I have submitted.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
There is a universal sentiment in this House adverse to the idea of any portion of our railroads falling into the
hands and under the control of American railway interests. There is no question as to that. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has that feeling in common with everybody, and we would all regret to know that any of our large and important railway undertakings had been, acquired in the interest of any railway corporation across the border. Why ? Because we would fear that Canadian interests would be jeopardized. My hon. friend has that fear and he thinks that a little clause in this Bill would probably prevent it in the case of the Canadian Northern Railway. It is because I cannot see that by any possibility we could prevent such a state of things occurring that I am against putting arty such clause in the Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Might I ask just for information : Does the minister believe that if there was a clause concerning American railways similar to that which prevents the Canadian Pacific Railway from amalgamating with the Canadian Northern Railway, that this company could amalgamate with an American company ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I have tried to answer the question before and to tell my hon. friend that a clause in the Bill such as he suggests would be just about as good as no clause at all; it would be no worse, it would be no better. They cannot under any circumstances amalgamate with an American railway unless they get power from this parliament to do it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: What is the use of saying that they cannot do a thing and shall not do a thing when they have no power to do it unless parliament says they may do it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I know of a Canadian railway that has been refused permission to cross the American frontier, and it has had to amalgamate with an American railway.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: True. We have in this parliament countenanced and legalized an amalgamation of two or three railways in particular, down in the Niagara district. But any legislation of this parliament would be helpless if men of capital acquired a controlling interest in the stock of any of our railway companies. The management would at once fall into their hands. Is any one in this parliament prepared to say that we ought to pass an Act declaring that none of the owners of shares in any of these corporations can assign their shares to any one ? Because the moment you assign or transfer the stock to any one, that moment you give up the control.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Is there any value in clause eight of this Bill ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: There is this value as between these two Canadian railways, that It Is notice to .them that they shall not amalgamate. But the most valuable part of the clause is not that they shall not amalgamate, but that they shall not enter into any agreement whereby rates shall be pooled.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: If we are going to have the Grand Trunk Pacific, why not have a similar provision in this Bill with respect to it ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Because it is not in existence.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: It is seeking an act of incorporation now.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: And when the Grand Trunk Pacific or any other company which is seeking legislation at our hands, asks for power to amalgamate with the Canadian Northern, then, if parliament has the feeling that it ought not to be done, it will not be done; and if parliament has the feeling that it ought to be done, it will be done, even though there may be a clause in the charter saying that the company shall not do it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Then, if the argument of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals is consistent, the position we should take is this, that if it is an advantage to Canada to have an additional transcontinental railway, and if we think it should uot amalgamate with the Canadian Pacific, then we should have a similar provision respecting the proposed Grand Trunk Pacific ; and if there is no such provision in this Bill, it should be in the Act of incorporation of the Grand Trunk Pacific which is before the House. I cannot see why the Canadian Northern should be prohibited from amalgamating with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and not be prohibited from amalgamating with the proposed Grand Trunk Pacific. Why should not the same rule be applied to both ? If the people of the west are to have the advantage of competition, why should we not render it impossible for the Canadian Northern to amalgamate with any other line ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: One reason is that the Grand Trunk Pacific, if it ever materializes, will be subject to the railway commission which is to be appointed, whereas the Canadian Pacific Railway cannot be, under the arrangement which was made years ago.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I understand, then, that this parliament is powerless to pass any legislation to prevent the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific from amalgamating. Is that the position we are in ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: No, not at all. I want to say that it appears to me we talk a good deal of nonsense in regard to American railways. When any Canadian company is organized, and receives a charter from this parliament to operate a railway, it becomes subject to the Railway Act of this Dominion, and therefore it does not make much difference whose money builds the road-it is a Canadian road subject to Canadian laws. How are you going to xirevent the stock of any corporation passing into the hands of Americans if they choose to buy it ? The stock is sold in the open market, and anybody who likes to buy it ean get control. The safeguard for the people of this country is that the road is a Canadian road under Canadian laws, and it does not matter who owns the stock. The difference between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific Railway is this. The Grand Trunk Pacific has not yet materialized; we do not know whether it is going to be built or not; but the Canadian Pacific Railway enjoys a monopoly under legislation of this parliament passed years ago, and we can have no control over the rates on its main line; whereas the Grand Trunk Pacific, if it is ever built, will be subject to the Railway Act, and the railway commission will have control over its rates. So that we do not want the Canadian Northern to amalgamate with the Canadian Pacific Railway because we have no control, whereas we do not care whether it amalgamates with the other or not, because we have control.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Then it seems to me that clause eight is only put in for effect, and that it is practically of little or no value. If it is an advantage to have two lines through that country, and a greater advantage to have three lines, why not make provision now, when incorporating another transcontinental line, to prevent it amalgamating with this road 1

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: We do not legislate in that way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
Probably not. It seems to me, however, that if this discussion has done nothing else, it has elicited the fact that the idea of aiding the Grand Trunk Pacific this session, at any rate, is at an end. The legislation which we are about to pass is legislation which was foreshadowed about fourteen months ago, in an announcement made by the premier respecting aid to this road. We are crystallizing into law a policy announced fourteen months ago; and the government have not progressed one step in the solution of the transportation problem since that time. I had the pleasure of being in the North-west last fall, and I can appreciate, from the point of view of the people living there, the importance of giving aid to this road. No-

body is opposing tlie granting of this aid; but we are objecting to tbe meagre information given by the government respecting their policy on this great transportation problem. There is no doubt that the roads the government are assisting by this Bill will be profitable almost from the moment they are completed, because they will pass through a most fertile country. Why does the government not elaborate its policy, and give further assistance to carry this road to the Pacific coast ? Let us have two transcontinental roads before we commence agitating for a third. I think that is a reasonable proposition, which ought to commend itself to the government. At any rate,
I am satisfied from the statements made by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) that this clause eight is of no practical value at all; and, that if the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific wish to come together, they can do so, so that a few years hence we may wake up to find that instead of having two transcontinental lines we have only one.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Just a word on that point. Does the hon. gentleman know that two railway companies incorporated by this parliament cannot amalgamate without special authority ? My own view is that the first three lines of this clause have practically very little legal effect. They may stand as a declaration of the policy of parliament; but inasmuch as no two railway companies can amalgamate, as has been pointed out by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, without a special Act of parliament, that lack of power would be just the same as if these two clauses were not there. As pointed out by the Minister of Railways and Canals, the important part of the clause is that which forbids any traffic arrangement except such as may be approved by the Governor in Council. So that, as a matter of fact, the views of the hon. gentleman and our views are practically the same. There is not much to dispute.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Are we not appointing a railway commission to regulate rates, and would they not have power to do that ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
Although this clause would have no legal value, I do not agree that it has no practical value. It has this practical value, that it is formally one of the conditions on which this aid is granted ; and if at any other time, one of these companies should come forward with a proposal to amalgamate, they would be met with the statement :	You knew at
the beginning that you received this aid on this condition. If parliament should see fit to waive that condition, of course this clause would have no legal effect, but it
is there as a notice of the desire and the intention of parliament and a declaration of the policy of parliament.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
That is just what I have in mind. It may be that this clause has no legal value now, but if parliament makes it a clear condition, that condition will have just the effect which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has stated.
I am asking parliament to declare that an amalgamation cannot be made with American railways any more than with the Canadian Pacific Railway. It seems; to me that if there be any reason for inserting this clause with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway, we should make it equally applicable to American corporations who may have designs on this Canadian railway. Such corporation will be aware of the fact that this parliament has pledged itself not to allow of any amalgamation. It will act as a warning, even if it has no legal value. We are about unanimous in granting the aid we are asked to give, and it seems to me that such a condition, as the one I am urging, should not be opposed, especially, in view of the fact that we are providing against amalgamation with the Canadian Pacific Railway. Mr. Hill's system is more to be feared than the Canadian Pacific Railway. If we fear the Canadian Pacific Railway to such an extent that we insert this clause, we should not hesitate in applying the same clause to American railways.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: And the Grand Trunk Railway.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: That is a horse of another colour. That is another question altogether. Perhaps we are -not proceeding on right lines at all. I am not sure that we are. My hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Sir. Davis) has just stated to the House what is in the minds of many people. He has led us to fear that our railways, which we are helping every year by *nillions, may some day be bought up by foreign corporations and managed in their interests. What he says is perfectly true. We cannot prevent a corporation placing its stocks and bonds in the markets of the world. Some two years ago, it was very well known to those who follow those matters closely, that Mr. Hill and other American capitalists were very seriously contemplating purchasing a majority of the Canadian Pacific Railway stock. "They tried to do so to the best of their ability, but as the Canadian Pacific Railway stock is scattered all over the world, it is very difficult to obtain control of it. The stock of a corporation like the Canadian Northern is. however, not so difficult a proposition. There is a good deal therefore in the argument of my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis). We are helping railways, we are pledging the credit of the country in their behalf, we are pledg-

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Supposing the stock of those railways passed into the hands of Americans to-morrow, would they not still be Canadian railways subject to Canadian laws, just as they are to-day ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: There is nothing more easy than for a railway company to carry its trade either to American or Canadian ports. Transportation from west to east means through-rates. Suppose Mr. Hill bought the majority of the stock in the Canadian Pacific Railway, the maritime provinces and even the port of Montreal would not see much of the western trade. He would naturally divert as much as he could to his own ports and railways.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: What line does Mr. Hill own into New York or Boston ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: He has connections with other American lines.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: What lines does he own ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: He has very fine lines to Duluth and St. Paul.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Might I ask the hon. gentleman another question ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
My hon. friend can speak when I am through. Here is the port of Duluth and near it is the Canadian port of tort William, here is Buffalo and here is Port Colborne-Buffalo on the one side and Port Colborne on the other. Mr. Hill has his organization on the lakes as on the land, and to-day he is carrying his trade to American channels. Not one pound of freight under his control goes through Canadian channels. Suppose he bought the Canadian Northern to-morrow, he would divert the traffic over that road to the American ports where all bis interests are centred. No one can doubt that. We are subsidizing railways right and left, we are prepared to give to anybody who wants to build railways, without making sure that the trade will be developed through Canadian channels. That is u mistake. I am not here to Hon. Mr. TARTE.
give advice to the government, and probably it would not be accepted, if I did ; but I hold such strong views on that point that I must express them. This country is growing, and it is bound to grow very fast, from east to west. Let us, then, keep this growing trade to ourselves. That is not asking too much, surely. We are not legislating for to-day. We are only six millions to-day ; but at the rate at which immigrants are coming in to the west and into all the provinces, we may be ten millions within a very few years indeed. I say again, let us manage our national business to-day in such a way that we shall not be reproached by those who come after us with having been imprudent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I do not wish to dissent from the ruling you gave befofe six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, though I feel like disagreeing with it to some extent. But before section 1 is adopted, I desire to ask tlie hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) a question. There is an impression throughout the country that the government have not settled their policy on the subject of transportation. Certainly, so far as this House is concerned we have no information. To give the House hope of being enlightened, and to satisfy the country as far as possible in the meantime,
I would like to ask the hon. minister if he hopes to be able at an early day to put the House in possession of the facts as to what the government policy is with regard to transcontinental lines ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Unless I am overruled by the committee, I must stand by the ruling I have made. I invite discussion of that rule, and, if I am overruled, I must submit with the best grace I can.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that I am neither discussing nor infringing the rule of the Chair. But I submit also that I have a right to ask a question, and I intend to avail myself of that right when any Bill is before this House.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I have no objection, if you will allow me, Mr. Chairman, to answer the bon. gentleman's (Mr. Sproule) question. It is the very strong hope and expectation of the government that, within a very few days, we shall be able to make an announcement to the country on the subject referred to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister if he sustains your ruling and is going to proscribe the discussion of the whole Bill in the committee ? I happened not to be in the House when the second reading was proposed, and so had not an opportunity to give my views upon it. I presume that if you, Mr. Chairman, adhere closely to your ruling, I shall be obliged to move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again, in order to have an opportunity to speak.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: 1 would point out to my kou. friend (Mr. Wilson) that we are now discussing the first clause and that clause contains the provision for the guarantee of the bonds of this road which is the essential feature of the whole matter. That affords pretty broad scope. I think there is no question but that the ruling of the Chair is correct, but that ruling would not preclude a discussion of all ^hat is covered by the first clause-and it covers the essence of the whole matter.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Then the kou. minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) does not object to a general discussion?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Within the limits of section 1.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: There is this to say-that a member of this House who speaks but seldom, is more apt to stray beyond the real question than one who speaks every day. I represent a rural constituency, one that is opposed to anything like bonusing a railway. My constituents feel that the time has come when it should stop. We have already bonused railways, I think, to the extent of $300,000,000, and ifr we

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: How many railways has the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson) in his riding ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
