subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I am very glad the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) has asked that question. For, on a previous occasion when I was discussing this point, I was twitted by the hon. Minister of Finance with the suggestion that I had in my constituency all the railways that were wanted. At that
time, we had 2i miles of railway that had been bonused. But since hon. gentlemen opposite came into power, who were pledged against bonuses, they have added six or seven miles of bonused railway. These are the only roads in my constituency that have been bonused.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: That is not an answer to my question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: What does the hon. minister wish to know ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: How many railways has the hon. gentleman In his riding ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Is that bonused ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: No, Sir.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Not bonused by Canada ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: No, if the hon. minister thinks it was, will he tell me when ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I am asking the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson).

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I can tell the hon. gentleman how it was bonused. I think he gave us an answer to that question himself. They were given a loan of $15,000,000 I believe. That was taken over at confederation at $25,000,000, and has been running ever since. I presume it represents about $100,000,000 that they owe now, and I guess, always will owe. Now, it is just this way :	I object to a few men getting
together, millionaires or others, forming a company, and coming to the government, and asking for a bonus for their benefit. I think that is unfair and undesirable. Besides that, we have the authority of the best railway men in this country and the United States for saying that where railways are required it is not necessary to bonus them, because where there is business for railways they will be built, money will be found to build them. Besides that, these gentlemen on the treasury benches, when they came into office, were strongly opposed to bonusing railways. I remember distinctly a letter that was written by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, in which he distinctly said that the policy of the Liberal party was against bonuses, and I think they got a good many votes all over Ontario on the strength of that. But since they have come into power, I think they have voted about $26,000,000 in bonuses, and I think they have paid out about

$11,000,000. The people in my section of the country think it is time this should come to an end. We have various farmers' institutes, or farmers' associations, in my riding which have been passing resolutions lately, and I think they sent one of their resolutions to the government asking that no more bonuses should be given to railways. They met on the 20th of June and also passed a resolution opposing any guarantees being given to railways. The feeling is that if it is a good thing the railway company will own it, but if it is a bad thing, we shall have to take it ourselves. I wish to say that X am entirely opposed to this way of doing things. Again, I see no provision in the Bill as to what is to become of the money when the railway promoters go to London to sell the bonds. These bonds are guaranteed by the government, and no doubt will sell well. Now I see no provision in the Bill as to what is to become of that money. I think it is a reasonable presumption that the railway men will control that as they like, that is to say, if this Bill is to be our guide. 1 do not think they should be allowed to do that, X think if we guarantee their bonds, the money should go into the hands of the government and should be paid out on progress estimates then we would be sure that the money would go into the building of the road. But if it goes into their hands -I am not going to say they will make an improper use of it-but they will have an opportunity of doing it if they like. Therefore, I wish to record my voice against this kind of aid to railways. Let the people who want to build railways furnish the money to build them. If it is thought that we must have railways and we cannot get them built in any other way, we had better build them ourselves and own them, rather than give bonuses like this. There is another trouble I see. The whole of this indebtedness is coming due at one time, at the end of fifty years. Now is it probable that this railway is going to put away a portion of its earnings every year to pay that large sum when it comes due ? I think if we are going to do this at all, there should be a Slinking fund so that they will pay so much a year, and you would have provided when the fifty years was up that money would be paid, and the government would not lie called upon to pay it.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I understood from the Minister of Railways that there was an understanding in that direction. I am with those who believe that that road, or any transcontinental road, should be a xiurely Canadian road. The Minister of the Interior said that it was unnecessary to compel this road, which had a more facile means of communication than passing through Minnesota, to go to the large expense of passing entirely through Canadian territory. He instanced the road that passes through the state of Maine to St. John. Let me remind the Minister of Railways and the Minister of the Interior of a fact which has been brought out in discussion lately, that where the path of communication, for either exports or imports, passes through a foreign country, that foreign country virtually controls the political existence of the country to which the road belongs. In all cases where it is possible. I think our railroads should pass exclusively through Canadian territory. The question arose lately in reference to the Bagdad Railway passing through Asia Minor to India, and the principle was laid down by the greatest thinkers that the country which controls the path of commerce controls the country where it originates. Therefore, w# should insist that this road should pass if possible through Canadian territory. The Minister of Railways said, oh, what is the difference ? What is to prevent American capitalists from purchasing the majority of the stock in a Canadian railway ? The purchase by a foreign corporation of a Canadian road does not give them the absolute control of the bonds. There are many means of control. For instance, we might insist that the majority of the directors of any railroad in Canada should be British subjects. That alone is sufficient to give us the control of our road, though the majority of the stock might be held by Americans. The minister says, well, what is the object of anything of that kind ? What is the object of a provision in an Act of parliament to prevent the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway from obtaining control of this road ? He says such a provision is useless in an Act of parliament. Before there could be an amalgamation with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway or any other railway, they would have to get authority from this parliament, not only before the owners could sell the road, but before they could transfer its control. Then

what is the use of putting that into an Act of parliament ? No use whatever. It is only a matter of show, only a matter of deceiving the public. The Minister of Finance said that this was a notification to the public generally, or to the people who invested in this road, that at no time would the Canadian parliament authorize a transfer of the Canadian Northern Railway to the Canadian Pacific Railway. But the parliament of Canada can at any time change that decision, and give authority to this road to sell or transfer any corporate powers that it possesses, or to amalgamate with the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway. Then a provision of this kind is useless in the Bill, it is only for the purpose of deceiving the public, the people of Canada who are investing their money in this undertaking. Then the Minister of Railways says that they can virtually obtain control of it. If they can virtually obtain control of it, what is the use of putting _ a provision of this kind In the Act V If they can get a majority of the stock and can get control of the institution, what is the use of making a provision of this kind ? There is no use whatever of putting it into an Act of parliament. Then, provisions of this kind are useless, because'the parliament of Canada can at any future time by legislation give to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, or the Canadian Pacific Railway, or any other railway, authority to amalgamate with this particular road. As to American roads, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals instanced some roads which the Americans at the present time have control of and which the parliament of Canada gave them control of. If they have obtained control from the parliament of Canada, parliament ought never to have consented to anything of the kind. The only legislation I am aware of that has been passed by the parliament of Canada is in reference to the bridge at Niagara Falls and to the electric road from Detroit to Niagara Falls, which has been given power to amalgamate with a Canadian electric railway company. It was wrong to allow them to do anything of the kind. The parliament of Canada should be very careful to prevent any American railway getting control of any corporate railway company in the Dominion of Canada. It is against the policy of the country. I warned the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals in the Railway Committee in reference to that particular subject. I warned him against giving power to any American railway to obtain control or to obtain corporate powers over a railway in the Dominion of Canada. One provision which should be embodied in the general Railway Act and in the charter given to any railway company in this country should be that a majority of the directors of the road should be British subjects.
Then, in reference to the general policy of the government we have not heard anything
from the hon. Minister of Railways or the Minister of the Interior. The hon. Minister of Railways states that upon a subsequent day shortly the policy of the government will be declared in reference to transportation and in reference to these transcontinental lines. But, here is a subject which peculiarly interests the people of the country. We are granting a subsidy to a transcontinental line. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and the hon. Minister of the Interior may say that the government have not considered their policy in reference to that. They should have considered it. They should have been prepared, when they brought down a motion for the purpose of assisting a transcontinental line, as I say this is, to state their whole policy in reference to transportation and in reference to transcontinental lines, and in reference as well to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, whose Bill is at present before this House. In connection with this Canadian Northern project they should have considered their policy in reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific as well as in reference to the question of the subsidy if it ever comes before this House. If we are to judge from the observations of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, we must conclude that this is abandoned for jthe present. Then, they should state the policy of the government as to whether they intend to abandon it or as to whether they intend to consider it in reference to the Canadian Northern. The jjarliament of Canada and the people of this country, when they are asked to subsidize 600 miles of road, or virtually to build it, because the amount of the subsidy is within $5,000 per mile of the cost as estimated by the department of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, are entitled to a statement from the government as to What their policy is in reference to the transcontinental system of roads and in reference to transportation from the North-west to this section of the country.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) one question before he sits down. He says that we should have in the Railway Act a provision that the majority of the directors of a railway in Canada should be British subjects. Take the case of the Kingston and Pembroke Railway. Mr. Flower, of New York, owns most of the stock. He appoints directors here in Canada, who are Canadians, to run the road and do ail the work. These are British subjects ; still, Sir. Flower runs the road to suit himself, because if these parties that he hired here did not do as he told them to do, they would be dismissed. I cannot see that there will be any particular advantage in having a provision of that kind incorporated in the Railway Act.

speechtext:
I can tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wrightl my opinion in reference to the matter. When a corporation

which has its entity in a foreign country and which, by the laws of this country, is enabled to obtain control of a railway in this country, and where you interfere with laws given to a foreign corporation, it becomes the corporate powers or rights which our laws give to a foreign corporation, it becomes then a question between Great Britain and the United States how far the investment in the entity or corporation which they receive from the American company is interfered with by legislation in lessening their interest or affecting it in any manner, and that is a strong reason why no corporation which has its power or entity in a foreign country should be allowed to obtain corporate powers over a railway in this Dominion of Canada.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I recognize fully what the hon. gentleman would like to protect, and I believe these interests should be protected. All I say is that I cannot see how he is going to protect it in the way he mentions.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must see that the entity or corporate powers which are given to a foreign company are entirely different from the corporate powers which we give to a similar institution in this country. If the corporate powers which are obtained in New Jersey or in New York give more extensive or greater powers than are given to a corporation in this country, the greater powers which they had obtained from New Jersey or New York state would be the governing or ruling powers over the corporation which had been obtained here, thus giving them an opportunity of obtaining wider powers than the powers which this parliament gave to the corporation or entity over which they have control.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wright) asks what advantage it would be if a director should be resident in this country. It seems to me that answer is a very simple one. A director who is a resident of this country would be held directly responsible to the courts of this country for any illegal act he did, while a director who lived in New York could escape the jurisdiction of the courts.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not rise for the purpose of obstructing this Bill in any sense. I think that, perhaps, seeing that these people were promised aid at the last session of the House, this Bill might go through with perhaps some amendments to it. I wish to refer to what was said this afternoon in regard to the traffic gathered by this railway west of Fort William or Port Arthur being diverted to American channels and American ports. I would like to draw the attention of the committee-I suppose the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals knows more about it than I do-to the fact that since the removal of canal tolls Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
this season and up to within a week ago more grain has gone over the St. Lawrence route than went down by that route during the whole of last season. I have the utmost confidence in the St. Lawrence route and in the fact that in future the great bulk of grain produced in the North-west Territories will find its way out by way of the St. Lawrence route. The reason that the grain has not been going down so much as we think it should have gone has been a lack of Canadian bottoms plying on the lakes. These ships, we are glad to know, are being built, and this year probably there will be twice the number operating that were operated last year. I think we may depend upon it that in future the outlet for the grain of the North-west Territories during the season of open navigation will be through the St. Lawrence route. I believe we will cope successfully with Buffalo and New York, and even now that is taking place. I wish in this connection to ask the Minister of Railways-and I ask the question because of so many rumours in reference to this line of railway being built by either the government or by a private corporation, from the city of Quebec to Winnipeg-I ask if the minister has any data or any surveys of this country at present in regard to the country through which this railway will pass ? Is it a country of mountains or an agricultural country ; is it fertile or is it barren ? Whether the government builds the road or whether it is built by a private corporation, it will be necessary for us to know what this railroad will cost approximately before entering into such a gigantic enterprise.

speechtext:
I am still in some doubt, Sir, whether the measure before us is being discussed as a transcontinental road or not. I understood that hon. gentlemen opposite at the beginning of this debate rather insinuated that they did not think the government had .made a sufficient announcement upon that point, but latterly, however, they have been discussing it as a transcontinental road. That being so, I am rather at a loss to understand why these gentlemen have not placed upon the Order paper the same kind of resolutions which they deem so essential in regard to that Bill which I had the honour to introduce into this House. If it is essential that a transcontinental road before being subsidized or aided by this government should require to have stipulated in its Bill, a clause that the directors and officers should be British subjects, I am amazed that that amendment is not now on the Order paper in connection with this Bill. If it is necessary that a transcontinental railway, whether it be an all-Canadian road or otherwise should find an outlet for its freight only through a Canadian port, I am also surprised that these hon. gentlemen who were suggesting that it was so essential in respect to another railway should not deem it as essential with regard to this railway. We had a very lengthy discussion in respect to another railway all of which pointed to the necessity of its being an all-Canadian road, or otherwise forsooth the Canadian parliament should not grant one dollar of aid. It was also suggested that rather than grant aid to that railway if it went to any other but a Canadian port, it should take a circuitous route and go 100 or 150 miles out of its way to reach a Canadian port, and thus transport its freight that additional mileage, and of course at an additional cost to our producers, or else it was not worthy of aid at the hands of the Canadian parliament. As 1 understand it these absolutely essential things for the other railway are not now suggested with regard to this railway. I did not agree with these propositions at the time; I do not agree] with them now. I believe that if we are to export successfully the products of this country, they must be borne to the sea-board by the shortest route in the shortest possible time and in the cheapest possible way. But Sir, I direct attention to the fact that we have none of these motions upon the Order paper to-day which were deemed to be so necessary before aid should be granted to the other railway. We have no stipulation that the terminus of this road must be a
Canadian port and that the freight originating on this line must be exiiorted through a Canadian port. Not only that, but we were told that any railway that is entitled to aid from this parliament should have a clause inserted in its subsidy Bill, or in some other Bill connected with it, that they should build the sections of the railway simultaneously and under the direction of the parliament of Canada. If that be true in respect to one railway, why is it not true in respect to another railway ? Why should not the rule apply to one railway as well as to another ? I am not objecting to the aid given to this Canadian Northern Railway, nor am I protesting against it in any way, but it is well known that their charters extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and yet in view of this transcontinental aspect of the line, some hon. gentlemen do not seem to think that the rules they apply to another suggested transcontinental railway should apply to this. I call attention to this simply because of the unparalleled length of the discussion that has taken place with respect to the Bill pertaining to another railway. Not only that, but when this other railway was not seeking aid so far as the parliament of Canada is advised, though there might be newspaper rumours to the effect that they might hope for aid or possibly that they might apply for aid-but only when they are simply asking for a charter, we are told by notices of motion and by lengthy speeches in the House

speechtext: In what form or to what extent the powers which belong to the government, as guarantors of the interest, shall be exercised, in case of default, is a matter which must he entirely in the discretion of the Governor General in Council. It is not intended that the government should tie its hands as regards the exercise of these powers. On the contrary the intention is to secure to the government all the rights which would belong to any one, under similar circumstances, in case the company made default in the payment of interest. I do not by this wish to suggest the government would consider that, in the early life of a road, it would be just and equitable to enforce its rights, whatever they may be, and I do not think that parliament would consider such drastic action as proper or fair treatment or that the company should not allow a reasonable opportunity to get its road into operation or establish its business before being treated as a defaulter. speechtext: I am aware that the hon. minister would not care to exercise the power of taking possession of the road or any of the powers which the bond-holders might exercise upon a simple default. The bond-holders, however, are paid their interest by the government, and they may not choose to part with the bonds. They may prefer to keep possession of them until the end of the fifty years, and the government will have to pay the interest during all that time. speechtext: But the bond-holders are in possession of the bonds, and the government can only exercise its rights on the understanding that it pays the shareholders the interest and the total amount of the bonds at the end of the fifty years.

speechtext: Default in the payment of interest would be a ground upon which the government would claim the right to take possession of the property, if it chose to do so, and operate the road.

speechtext:
I understand that the government are going to put in the

5G32
mortgage the right to exercise the power of taking possession at any time the company is in default, just as the bond-holders would do.

speechtext: Quite so. But I am not going to say that we will arbitrarily stipulate that that power must be exercised in one, two or three years. The government will reserve the power to do so according to the arrangements stipulated in the mortgage.

speechtext: And to prevent any other lieu.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.

point without having had an opportunity to consider it. It does not alter the case here, because we take our second security on the other portions of the line as an additional security. That being a prior lien upon the line mentioned, foreclosure of that mortgage would cut out the second charge of this government upon those lines, but upon those lines only, leaving His Majesty in right of the government of Canada with a prior lien

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I can understand that the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) wished to know what we would do in such a case -whether we would take over the property, and so on. I could not answer that now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Whether the government would buy in at a foreclosure sale-I suppose that would depend on circumstances.

speechtext: I could not answer that question now.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I understand the hou. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) to be directing his attention not to the question of what the government would do if that contingency arises, but what steps they were taking now to protect themselves and the people in case of a difficulty arising with regard to the Manitoba mortgage.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The only thing that occurs to me is that possibly, parliament might give us power to raise sufficient money, when the contingency arose, to buy the lines in.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
What I understand the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) to direct his attention to is not what the government would do when the difficulty arises, but what precaution the government proposes to take now in getting this security to protect themselves in case the railway company should default in regard to that prior claim. Now, it is unfortunate, I think that the government have not brought down to the House some general outline, at all events, of the scheme they propose as a matter of security to the government. There have been several pertinent remarks from this side of the House, and I understand that what we want, so far as we can, is to have an assurance from the minister that proper steps will be taken, so that, if the

default happens in the payment of interest or anything of that kind, there may be the means in the hands of the country to protect the interest of the people. The hon. minister, a few minutes ago, gave a reply which was in this line-that he did not assume that the government would like to tie its hands by saying they would immediately act upon default. That I can well understand. X do not think that this House would want them to act hurriedly in case of some slight delay in the payment of interest. But what I understand we would like to have the government keep in mind in completing this transaction is that the necessary stipulations be put in the document drawn up, so that the government may be in a position, in case of default, to secure themselves and the people they represent. It is not necessary that these stipulations and provisions should be immediately exercised, but there should be such terms in the mortgage as to enable the government to control the situation when it arises, if it does arise. If that is done, we shall have no ground to complain with regard to the government, but if it is not done, we shall have great ground to complain. And, if we on this side fail to call the attention of the government to this point at the present time, the people will have great ground of complaint against us. I think it is to be regretted that this document, in outline, at all events, has not been submitted to parliament. But as it has not been, the duty will much more rest upon the minister and upon the government to see to it that there are such stipulations in it as will enable the government to control the situation in case of default.
Now, I would like to direct attention to another point, and that is with regard to what the hon. minister said a few minutes ago about payments-that he would not expect the railway company, within a few years, to be able to do anything towards reducing this indebtedness. That I would anticipate. I understand from the intention expressed by the minister that the railway company are not to be called upon to pay the bonds to the parties advancing the money for fifty years. Yet, it is not inconsistent with that provision that protection should be afforded, either by a deposit with the government or some other way, that there shall be some reduction of the indebtedness far short of fifty years. I think it is very desirable that that should be provided for, beginning within a reasonable number of years so that there shall be a regular and continual reduction of the indebtedness and, at the end of fifty years, it shall be substantially reduced.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Can the hon. minister state whether or not there is to be any provision in the mortgage for a sinking fund at any time ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I am not in a position to state definitely that there will be. I have already stated to the committee that that is a matter which is being considered. Hon. members are aware that in nearly all these great and successful railway undertakings the jjlan adopted is to retire the bonds as rapidly as possible, and make an issue of perpetual guaranteed stock. We all know from experience of railway corporations that the original debt or bond issue which has been incurred is not repaid. It stands against the property. The reason for not repaying it is not that the company might not be able to repay it, might not constitute a sinking fund which would in time wipe out the debt, but because demands-legitimate demands- are ever arising for the extension in all directions of the railway, the enlargement of its works, the increase of its capital expenditure. Instead of retiring the bonds, the company uses the means which would go to the retirement of those securities in the construction of new works and the carrying out of necessary improvements which are incidental to the work of every great railroad. I think that the government, perhaps, will not insist on a sinking fund, for the reason I have stated. It may be that when we get down to details it will be agreeable to both parties that guaranteed stock should be issued, and, retire all the bonds by the expiration of the fifty years. That may be agreed upon as being the best method of concluding the arrangement. All these things require to be canvassed and discussed fully, but we have first to get the authority of parliament in order to know that we could go on with the undertaking and give the guarantees which are necessary in the first instance. So I would not wish to be understood as making any more precise or definite statement on that subject. The committee may rest assured that no course will be taken except such as will absolutely guarantee the country from any possible loss on any securities which we take.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: It is because the information is meagre that we have endeavoured to ascertain what is the understanding between the government and the company. It seems to me there has been no agreement reached in regard to details at all.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I would like to ask the minister whether he proposes, under this clause, to ask the House to authorize the government to guarantee the interest in per-



petuity upon any debentures that are issued ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: No, not at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Well, you have power under this clause.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: No, we take it that, we are limited as to the term for which our guarantee is to continue ; it cannot exceed fifty years. But it does include a guarantee of the principle as well as the interest, of course. But if it should ultimately transpire, when the arrangement is concluded that an issue of guaranteed stock is to be substituted for these bonds, to retire the bonds at maturity, that guaranteed stock would not be covered by any government guarantee. It would only be a new guarantee the same as the stock issued by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and which is authorized to be issued by various other companies, some of which have received their authority during the present session.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: No matter what view the government may take, or we may take of it, we know the view that a company such as is being formed will take of this. While they are able to borrow the money of this country at three per cent they are not at all likely to borrow money at four per cent to take up these bonds. The transaction that we are going into is one that will last for fifty years. That should be well understood at the present time, because other corporations are coming to the government, this matter is going to be extended, and it should be well considered. When you are loaning money for fifty years to this company at three per cent, yon cannot well refuse a loan under similar circumstances to other institutions probably for a much larger sum. This country is going to become the banker at this very low rate of interest, I might almost say for all time to come, not only for this institution but for similar ones organized for the purpose of opening up the North-west, and for that great system of transportation which the government have had under consideration ; so that this loan may develop into an enormous sum. The government should consider that they are loaning money on terms which will incite others to come and ask for the same advantage. It is not like that kind of security that you can take to a bank or financial center and raise money upon it. This company has got to finance these bonds, not only through the present good times, but through all kinds of times that we may have during the next fifty years, probably many more years.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman surely understands that the government are not responsible for financing these bonds.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: You are, because without your endorsation these bonds could not lie financed.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: That is true, but this is a totally different proposition to saying that the government are bound to see that these bonds are financed at a rate which means three per cent interest only. That means that the bonds must necessarily sell at par, I hope they may, it would be much to the advantage of the company that they should. Of course, if the bonds were being issued by the government itself, if we were making a loan and were issuing these bonds bearing three per cent interest, undoubtedly they would be good at par. But whether in an indirect way we guarantee the company holding these endorsed securities, is a matter to which I do not feel free to state with confidence for a moment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The government surely consider that when they endorse a bond they are responsible for it.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Undoubtedly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: And the bond to all intents and purposes is their own bond, and if that bond can be negotiated in the markets of the world at three per cent, it is not at ail likely that an individual company will think for a moment of taking these bonds up, because they won't be able to go into the market and raise money at the same rate. Therefore I wish to impress upon the House and the country that what the government are doing at the present time is lending money, they are lending their credit, which is the same thing, to this company to build this road, and that the security' they hold is the road itself, a road which I believe will be built for a few thousand dollars more than the government are guaranteeing. Under these circumstances I think the government should do as bankers would do. They not only want to know that they are going.to get their interest, but they, want to know how these bonds are going to be financed, they want to know the aranngements that are being made by this company for financing the bonds ; because the company do not pretend that they can pay this interest from the very date of the bonds, they have got to carry them for some little time. So the government should be assured that they are at once going to commence to pay interest upon them, and the company are going to finance them in such a way that the government will not be called upon, at any rate until the company have developed the new resources of the railroad, in such a way as to make this a good investment.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I think myself that this government may very properly interest itself in this direction-I have had it in my mind for

a long time-as to the manner in which these bonds will be disposed of, not because we would be responsible for any more than we guarantee, because we are really not obliged to pay any more than the face of the bonds on maturity. We would naturally desire, in the interest of the undertaking itself, and in the interest of our security, that the bonds should realize the highest possible amount so that all that money should go into the undertaking. The larger the amount that goes into the undertaking, the better the security will be. I can say to my hon. friend that this matter will not be lost sight of by the government, and that we shall look after the manner in which these bonds are financed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I may point out that it is possible that several hundred miles of this road might be built, and then the company might collapse, they might meet with great trouble in the financial market and might not be able to continue it. The government should, under these circumstances, say that they should have enough on hand to go on and finish the undertaking, because an unfinished undertaking is worthless. I think we are entering upon an expenditure that is likely to become very serious indeed, and that the government cannot take too many securities. We on this side of the House are very desirous that no stumbling block should be placed in the way of this company carrying out their undertaking, because we believe it to be largely in the interest of the country. Personally I have the greatest possible objection to piecemeal legislation and piecemeal railways. I think all this should have been done as part of that great plan of transportation that was suggested three years ago, and that we should have had our commissioners at work by this time, and this whole thing should have been thrown upon their shoulders. As it is at present, the government are taking upon their shoulders a good deal of the work that this commission should have had to do. But by the time they have appointed their commissioners and these have got to work, the government will have committed itself to such an extraordinary undertaking that the commissioners will find their hands tied by the time they get into office. I think that the government, on their own behalf as well as in the interest of this country, cannot take too many securities at the present time that this enterprise they have entered upon shall be so conducted as to make it safe for the country.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I would like to bring the hon. minister's attention to the question of a sinking fund. The answer which the hon. minister gave to the hon. leader of the opposition makes it pretty clear that at the present time the government have no intention of requiring that anything should be done in the way of a reduction of this debt 1771
within the period of fifty years. The hon. minister says that at the end of fifty years there will be no renewal of the security by the government, that the railway will have to pay this debt off by negotiating other bonds. He says that the government will then be free of it and that the railway company will have to carry on the indebtedness. That is all very well if it works out in that way, but whether it does or does not depends upon the position of the railway company at that time. If the government take the position in arranging the security that there is to be no sinking fund in the meantime, they are leaving it to chance as to whether they can get rid of the security at the end of fifty years. They will be confronted with this position that in the event that the railway company cannot then negotiate the security without the endorsement and guarantee of the government-and they are very likely not to be able to negotiate the security unless the government will endorse it from the fact that parties loaning money will look for a guarantee from the government-if the railway company cannot then negotiate the security without the aid of the government, the government will either have to again guarantee the security or else they will have to take the railway property into their own hands. I think that is a very unwise position in which to leave us. At the end of fifty years and long before fifty years have expired, we ought to be getting into the position that our liability will be less and less. We have control of this in the beginning and now is the time to make provision for the contingency which I speak of. We cannot shut our eyes to the fact that there are other railways which will expect the same thing from us and which will be entitled to receive it. I am,not objecting to aid being given to this company if proper security is taken, but what I wish to impress upon the government is that there is a necessity in this case, having regard to the circumstances that we will be incurring other liabilities for other railways and in proportion as we increase our liabilities the credit of Canada will decrease, that something should be done within the period of fifty years, and beginning within a period of a few years-say twenty-five years-in the way of a reduction of this indebtedness. Otherwise, the government have no guarantee whatever that this money will be forthcoming without the aid of the government at the end of fifty years. I want to call the attention of the hon. minister and of the committee to the danger that threatens us in dealing with this matter. It would hardly have taken as long to prepare a document as it has taken us to discuss this measure by reason of the vague way in which it is brought before us. I believe this committee was resting upon the implied assurance of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals that there

would be a decrease in the liability by means of a sinking fu*d or something of that kind and that that idea prevailed amongst hon. members. Until the hon. leader of the opposition got up and pointedly put the question to the hon. minister I believe this committee were quite prepared to believe that we were going to have a provision when the arrangement was carried out that would secure us in the line I have mentioned by having a sinking fund to diminish our liability from year to year. I do not mean that the hon. minister wished to mislead the committee, but he was allowing it to go in silence after I had asserted the fact and only for that pointed question we would probably all have gone away with the understanding that the government had undertaken that there would be a sinking fund. I think we must ask the hon. minister to make as definite a statement as possible as to what will be done in the way of securing us in the document. that will be drawn up.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I am surprised to hear the remarks which my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) has made. I do not think my hon. friend realizes that this country has any future at all. I do not think he has the slightest conception of the magnificent territory through which this road is to pass. I do not think he realizes that the road will be one of the most profitable railways on this continent, which it will be by reason of the fact that it passes through a splendid fertile belt capable of almost continuous settlement from Winnipeg right up to Edmonton, to which point we are carrying the line. Almost the whole of the country for many miles on both sides of the line is susceptible of settlement. The hon. gentleman cannot have the slightest conception of the value which this property will acquire in a very few years to come. He talks about our requiring a sinking fund for our protection. It may be, on consideration, possibly desirable to provide for a sinking fund, but it may be infinitely better that the surplus earnings of the road should be expended upon the road in increasing the accommodation given to the public and in increasing the facilities that the public will require. I would not undertake to give the committee any assurance that we would insist upon the diversion of any portion of these earnings instead of ensuring their expenditure upon the undertaking itself. I think my hon. friend will, on reflection, see that it will be tying the hands of the government to an unreasonable degree, and that it would possibly be doing an irreparable injury to this great undertaking if we were to provide that the surplus earnings of the undertaking should be expended in the manner he suggests.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I am glad the hou. minister has waxed eloquent over the enormous resources of this country ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Do not believe it ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I will tell the hon. minister in a moment if he will allow me, whether I believe or not. It may be that I have for a moment been forgetful of the resources and the promise of this country, and of the prospect that this country will occupy a position greater than any of us can dream of at the present time. Those who are accustomed to wealth ari apt to forget it. Belonging to the Consei vative party, the one party that has always believed in the future' of this country, that has always believed in the west, that has always believed in the great advantage of a transcontinental railway, I say, belonging to such a party, basking in the wealth of knowledge which the Conservative has possessed in the past, it is not surprising that I have for a moment forgotten the affluence with which we are surrounded, but, the hon. gentleman, belonging to the party which in the old days had a poverty of appreciation in that regard, which believed that country would never support one, let alone three or four transcontinental railways, belonging to a party which has suddenly come to realize what this country can produce, I think, he is carried away and that he is like a man who has suddenly come into a fortune. If I had not so much respect for the hon. gentleman I would suggest that he had almost lost his head. He gave us a very reasonable picture when he supposes that this railway is going to be a paying enterprise, that it will be a success, that there will be the best kind of trade for it to do, that there will be a vast amount of commerce for it to transport. This is all the more reason why the company should, while they are piling up money from year to year, as I hope and believe they will, liquidate this indebtedness. As they go along and wish to make extensions^ adding to their rolling stock and equipment in various ways, they can do so, and being in good credit they can finance in such a way as to form a sinking fund and at the same time carry out their enterprise with success. I do not question the stability or success of this enterprise, but we are entering upon a career in which we may be called upon from time to time to make similar grants, and I do not want that the country should be adding to its liabilities from year to year without end making no provision for curtailing them. In five, in ten or in fifteen years as we incur increasing liabilities, I want that we shall have coming into the treasury something from the earlier grants which we have made, so that our indebtedness shall not climb up to an extent

which would uot be sanctioned by a prudent people such as the Canadian people are.

speechtext: I will be very happy to do it.

speechtext: 1 would not call it a ' mass ' of material.

speechtext: I know that my hon. friend is afflicted with the disease which seems to have affected a good many; of his friends; that is, the old story of saying that the minister does not know anything. I think we have managed to show that we have some knowledge of what we are doing and that we are conducting matters in a fairly businesslike way; so much so that my hon. friend has very little ground for successful criticism.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I am only measuring the hon. gentleman's knowledge by what he has stated himself.

The hon. gentleman would be quite ready to make the same observation if he were to ask me for a further array of impossible things. The hon. gentleman does not suppose that the government has nothing else to do during the session, but
sit down and work out the minutiae of all these matters.

speechtext: What about the Yukon contract ? Youi were able to do that.

It is quite impossible for the; ministry to give attention to these details during the session of parliament. I think you will find that when we come to deal with the matter we will be able to work it out satisfactorily to the country, even though our friends opposite may not admit it is satisfactory to them.
