If it escapes our attention and if the hon. gentleman calls attention to it my hon. friend will bring them down immediately.	v
On section 7,-running powers to other lines.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
This clause provides that the Governor in Council may grant running powers over some portions of this line in favour of other railway companies and upon terms considered equitable. If this railway company wishes to get some terms of relief from the position it may be in, it will be very easy to get somebody to suggest that running powers would be very desirable in favour of a particular railway, and the government may give certain concessions on such terms as are expedient and equitable, in consideration of the running powers being allowed. In that way, in the time of difficulty this company might induce the government-I do not mean to say that the present government could be induced to do anything that might be improper, but there might be another government not sp careful of the country's interests as the present one, and they might be induced as a consideration for granting runnibg powers over a portion of this line to do something that would interfere with the security of the country for the guarantee they have given. For example, if this country had advanced a million dollars or two million dollars, the government could make a stipulation that in consideration of their allowing running powers for a short distance upon the line, the country should wipe out all that liability. I would suggest to the minister, in the interest of the country, that he should add to this section some such words as these. ' But without impairment of the security of the government ' or any

words of that kind that will protect the country against the release of any rights which it has under the guarantee.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I am unable to grasp the possibilities or the probabilities that my hon. friends foresees may possibly occur which would affect prejudicially the value of the government security in operating under that clause. I confess that I cannot see how it could possibly arise.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I would suggest one or two ways in which it could arise. The owners of this subsidized road might ask the government, in consideration of running powers being granted on one part of the line, to release or discharge the lieu or mortgage on the other parts. If the contracting party which gets running powers has to pay something to this company for the running powers, that is one thing ; but if the government has power to release the securities, that is another thing. I think it would be reasonable to say that whatever terms might be made for granting running powers, those terms should not be such as would result in an impairment of the value of the security under which this guarantee is granted.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: There is nothing which the hon. gentleman has suggested, nor which I think he can suggest, which would have the effect under this clause of impairing the value of the security which the government would have power to give without the authority of parliament. My hon. friend might almost as well say that we ought to have a clause in this Bill providing that the government should not some morning declare that the mortgage was paid and had ceased to be a security of costs. The one case is as sup-posable as the other. No government could do it. A government cannot extinguish any claim which is due, or discharge any security without payment. If it attempted to do it, the claim would be nevertheless enforced. Parliamentary authority is required ; my hon. friend must admit that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: There is not a word here regarding parliamentary authority.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: No, because my hon. friend is contemplating that running powers would be given to some other company which offered as a condition to this company to consent that one-half the claim of the government against them should be cancelled. Where can power be found to reside in the government to extinguish any portion of that claim other than by actual payment ? When this clause speaks about equitable terms, it means that the company which requires the right to use these tracks shall pay in an equitable way and according to equitable conditions-not that the company which gives this mortgage to us shall receive from
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: the government or from anybody satisfaction for their security, but that they shall receive from the company which gets the right to run over their tracks proper consideration for the privilege they obtain.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The clause provides, not that this company shall grant running powers, but that the Governor in Council may grant running powers on terms that may be considered equitable. The consideration of the grant will pass as between the government and this railway company, and in consideration of the government doing that, they may release the company which is guaranteed from any liability which they have against them.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: My hon. friend must know that even without that clause, under the ordinary clause found in the Railway Act to-day, and which has been there for years, the Governor 'in Council, through the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, has the right to grant running powers to one company over another company's lines on terms that may be considered equitable. Strike this clause out, and the general law would still hold it. The only reason it is here, is that it may appear in the terms of the agreement as one of the conditions of the guarantee, giving it a contractual character, in addition to the ordinary legal sanction which is found in the Railway Act. Does the hon. gentleman want to leave the Railway Act without any provision of that kind ? Because if he has any warrant for his anxiety on that point, he cannot permit the Railway Act to continue with that clause in it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The difficulty of my hon. friend from Hamilton arises because in one of the clauses you give the Governor in Council power to deal with the securities, and'in this clause, though from another standpoint, you give the Governor in Council power to deal with the question of granting running powers over portions of the railway, and you have these words added, ' upon terms considered equitable.' My hon. friend is not arguing that the government can without statutory authority do anything to impair the security, but he is arguing that the terms you are using here might carry the action of the government to that extent.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think it would ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The Governor in Council, under section 7, might inadvertently place the country in such a position that the powers otherwise exercisable under this guarantee would be stayed for a time.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
How is it possible to conceive that a company, which owned this railway subject to guarantee, and which was asked

to give to an outside company permission to run over its tracks, should pay that other company ? Would not the contribution he from the other company to that company ? Then, how Is any contribution which is to be made by the new company going possibly to work an impairment of the security which the government holds under this guarantee ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: What 1 imagine my hon. friend from Hamilton has in mind, and what has occurred to myself, is that powers might be granted, under the very comprehensive expression used here, that would not be prejudiced by any encumbrance that might be placed on the road, and the government might find itself, by reason of the powers created by section 7, in a position not to enforce its security for a certain time at least. I am not prepared to say at the moment whether or not that result might be accomplished under section 7, but I can see enough in it to justify my hon. friend from Hamilton in bringing it to the notice of the government. There is another thing in section 7 which strikes me as rather peculiar, that is, that it seems to retain in the Governor in Council a power which the Bill at present before the House purports to vest in another body.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I think the words ' Governor in Council ' might just as well be struck out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I would think so, otherwise you are creating two bodies of equal authority to deal with that particular matter. The scope of the Railway Commission Bill before the House is that all such powers shall no longer be exercised by the Governor in Council, but by the hoard of Railway Commissioners.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The Railway Committee of the Privy Council can do it, but I have no objection to strike the words out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
That would remove perhaps to a considerable extent the force of what my hon. friend from Hamilton has suggested, because the Raihvay Committee of the Privy Council has not under the terms of a Railway Act, nor has the Board of Railway Commissioners under the Bill now before the House, any authority to in any way impair the security created by this measure.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved that the words ' the Governor in Council or' and the word 'also' be struck out of section 7.
Clause, as amended, agreed to.
On section 8,
It shall be unlawful for the Canadian Northern Railway Company to lease or sell any of its lines or any portion thereof to the Canadian
Pacific Railway Company, or to amalgamate with the said company, or enter into any agreement with the said company whereby rates upon freight or passengers shall be pooled ; but this provision shall not extend to traffic or running arrangements made with the assent of the Governor in Council.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: There was a great deal of discussion on this clause when we were dealing with clause 1. Whether the first part of the clause has any legal effect or not, whether it is to be regarded as a formal notice or otherwise, it seems to me that no reason has been advanced for the insertion of this provision, so far as the Canadian Pacific Railway is concerned, which would not be equally potent with regard to any other railway company. Although I followed pretty closely the remarks of the hon. Minister of Railways and the hon. Minister of the Interior, I was not able to gather from them any reason which would justify the existence of this clause, so far as the Canadian Pacific Railway is concerned, which would not equally justify its existence so far as every other railway company is concerned. I would be glad if the hon. minister would say a word on that point.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
There are two branches of this clause, concerning each of which a different line of observations might properly be made. The first portion is that which refers to the sale or amalgamating of the Canadian Northern with the Canadian Pacific Railway. This clause, in a different form but in precisely the same spirit and with precisely the same purpose, seems to have been adopted in almost all the legislation of a general character which has been passed both in this parliament and the provincial legislature of Manitoba. It is in conformity, therefore, with the previously expressed desire of parliament that this provision is inserted. I have no doubt that such a provision has been always made because it was felt that the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is a very powerful corporation financially, might conceive that it would be desirable to acquire the Canadian Northern and control it, and if in no other way that control could be secured, it might desire to control it by means of the acquisition of the Canadian Northern stock. Parliament did not leave that an open question for a later parliament to determine, but, so far as an Act of parliament could have any effect upon the actions of succeeding parliaments. this parliament has made it one of the conditions of the charter that the Canadian Northern should not pass its property over to the Canadian Pacific Railway. This no doubt was due to the strong western feeling that there should be two distinct railway corporate interests serving that country, and that they should not be allowed to unite to the disadvantage of the shippers in that territory, and to avoid such

ii possibility, parliament was asked to include that restrictive clause in any legislation it might pass. The same feeling does not exist with regard to any other possible combination. The North-west will have two great roads when this road is completed, and will thus have the benefit of competition, and there is no necessity for passing legislation which would anticipate something that may never happen. I cannot see any reason why the Canadian Northern should not amalgamate with any other company except the Canadian Pacific Railway nor why any other company should not amalgamate with the Canadian Northern. There would be nothing detrimental to the public interest, should either event take place, and should any such proposal arise in the future, we will be able to deal with it. It is wise always to legislate no further than the reasonable needs of the moment require, and it is not wise to endeavour to provide for too remote a period in the future. It would not be wise for us to say now that we should not allow the Canadian Northern to amalgamate with any other company or any other company to amalgamate with it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Why not ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
Why should we ? Why should not the Canadian Northern have the privilege of adding to the strength of its road by uniting with another system ? Why should it not have the privilege of uniting with the Grand Trunk Railway if it wanted to do so ? At all events, it is a very proper thing for parliament to wait until the time comes when the companies exist and those companies want to have an amalgamation. When that time comes parliament will have the power to decide it; it cannot be done without the decision of parliaments What is the use, then, of our projecting ourselves into the future to deal with a ease that may never arise, and with which, if it should arise, we must deal according to the ideas and temper of parliament when the case is before it. Therefore, in my judgment, there is no reason why we should deal with this question now. When that request is made, it will be for the parliament of that time to deal with it. There is another phase' 6} this case which has value and importance in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway. And that is the clause which says that it shall be unlawful for this company to enter into any agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway! Company whereby rates upon freight or passengers shall be pooled. Such an arrangement would be equivalent in practice to an amalgamation ; and the object is to prevent that, so that there shall be the fullest advantage to the public which can accrue from competition. Now, we could not say properly-it would be a very great mistake in legislating for us to say-that under no terms should the Can-Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
adian Northern be allowed to make a pooling arrangement with any other road. It might be necessary for them to make pooling arrangements with companies. They run alongside the Canadian Pacific Railway and reach practically the same destination. Therefore, it is very much in the public interest to forbid pooling with that company. But I can conceive of companies existing in Canada with which it would be very much to the advantage of the Canadian Northern to have a pooling agreement, say, after the traffic had left their line and was being carried to its destination by land. It would be very desirable to make a pooling arrangement, subject to the approval of the constituted authorities, which would sit in judgment on such an arrangement. It would be a great advantage to the shippers. So we could not use that general language with regard to pooling arrangements, and it would not be wise for us to say that the company should not make such an arrangement with any other companies. It would tie their hands In carrying on the business of the company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
On division.
On section 9,
Any moneys paid by the government of Canada under the guarantee herein provided for shall be held to be paid in discharge of the liability of the government but not in discharge of the liability of the company under the securities so guaranteed or under the mortgage securing them, and the moneys so paid shall be held to be still secured by the said securities and mortgage, and the governmnt shall be subrogated in all the rights of the holders of the securities the interest upon or the principal of which has been paid by the government, and the government shall in respect of all moneys so paid be in all respects in the position of security holders in respect of whose securities default has been made in payment to the extent of the moneys paid by the government.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I think the word ' the ' before the words ' interest upon or the principal of which has been paid ' should be struck out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: It is all right there.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: It is better expunged.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: You want a comma after ' security.'

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Shall the amendment be adopted ? Carried.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
I suppose it is quite clear that under this section, however great the payments of the government may be upon these securities, and however long the government may have to wait for the return of the money, the government gets no interest, but simply has the position of the holder of a coupon which bears no interest. If the government advanced say $2,000,000 in the

course of a few years in taking up coupons, they could not recover interest. I want to know exactly wliat the intention of the government is, because it seems to me quite clear that however large these payments, or however long the government must wait, it gets no interest upon its money.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's (Mr. Barker's) inference, assuming that this section covers all that the government would stipulate and include within the mortgage terms, is correct-there is no provision here for the payment of interest upon interest.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I mean it does not give the government the right to it, if they wish to claim it.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: This clause does not pointedly contemplate that, but this clause by no means exhausts the power of the government in defining the terms and conditions upon which the line may be guaranteed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: The hon. minister lias again used the expression that the government are not charging interest upon interest. I should think it would be unnecessary to point out that, though this is interest as between the bondholders and the company, it is not interest as between the company and the government. The government must pay this interest and, as between the government and the company, it then becomes principal. Has the hon. minister anything to say to the committee as to the terms of the mortgage in this respect ? Will it be dealt with in the proposed mortgage ? Is it the intention of the government to pay large sums under this without having the right, if they desire to exercise it, to recover interest, at the rate expressed in the agreement, from the company while these sums remain unpaid ? Of course, it may be a very serious matter. The government may pay $250,000 or $275,000 per annum four or five years and this might remain for five or ten years longer unpaid. Therefore, it is a matter of some moment to consider, either now or hereafter. I do not know whether or not the hon. minister has made up his mind and is able to offer the committee any information with regard to it.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I can only say that this is a question that, with many others, must arise in working out the details, and it will have to be considered and dealt with by the government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
The government, I believe, occasionally have to borrow money from the banks, for which they pay five per cent. They may borrow money at five per cent to take up some of these three per cent securities. To get money to pay the three per cent, they may be obliged to pay five per
cent. The government should obtain the power to charge what the money costs.
The MINISTER) OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. That is a very proper subject for consideration.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: There is another reason why I would call the attention of the Minister of Railways to this point. It is usual on these railway mortgages to provide that on default no proceeding shall be taken by the trustees except upon demand of 66 or 75 per cent of the bondholders. Therefore I think the government, after advancing $1,000,000 at any rate, should be in a position to enforce the mortgage under the ordinary form of a trust mortgage, unless it can obtain the consent of two-thirds or three-fourths of the bondholders, who may be quite willing to leave the government out of this money, and leave them out for many years. It is necessary for that reason that the government should protect itself, and I have no doubt that the minister will see to it.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I would ask the minister if he has considered the proposition that was thrown out here when we were considering the resolutions, in reference to providing for the government being able at any time to take over the road and everything in connection with it, and to provide means whereby the value of the road and that sort of thing might be ascertained. I may say there is a feeling in our country at least that the time is coming when it will be necessary for the government to take over any undertakings of this kind, and we should at this time provide the machinery for so doing. I understand that the government at all times have power, by exercising what the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) calls the principle of eminent domain, to take over any railway. In this case, I think provision should be made in the Bill so that if the government wish at any time to take over this road, they may have the means of arriving at a valuation of the same, and taking possession. That was discussed a while ago on section 8 of the Bill with reference to an amalgamation with the Canadian Pacific Railway. This will be a further safeguard, because the government would have it in their hands at any time, if anything should happen such as the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) mentioned the other day, to take the road over and run it as a government property.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
Any suggestion of that kind, if adopted at the present time, would interfere seriously with the floating of these bonds that you are guaranteeing. I think it would have a serious effect if the government took power to assume possession of this road. Are the government going to be the debtors, and have these bonds issued to bond-holders, holding them for fifty

years from the government of Canada ? I think the government would place themselves in a very invidious position, particularly in view of the fact that there is a scheme for a transcontinental railway at the present time. You are going to have one part of the road tied up under one set of conditions, and you don't know whether a future parliament would be able, under these conditions, to take over another portion of the road and to make it continuous to the Pacific. The fewer conditions you put in the better.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: If the country's credit is good, and we guarantee the interest at 3 per cent on these bonds, the credit of the country is all right, and it does not make much difference what conditions we are putting in the Bill. The bondholders will look to the government that guaranteed the principal and interest, and it won't make any difference whether you put that in or not.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) perhaps misapprehends the tenor of the remarks made by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock). The hon. member for Toronto sees a difficulty which I must confess impresses my own mind at the moment. He is proposing a measure of which it will be open to the government to avail itself in fifty or one hundred years from now, when the company might be desirous of floating securities in substitution of those which have been guaranteed by the government. The power is one not confined by any statutory limitations. It would be open to the government at any time to avail itself of the opportunities and the special means of ascertaining the value of the property, if it wished to take it over. Now I must say to my hon. friend from Saskatchewan that that proposition has not been considered, and I am not in a position to make any statement as to what vfould be the action of the government upon it. But I would suggest to the hon. member that we are now dealing with what perhaps will be for all time but a fraction of a considerable railway system, we are dealing with six or seven hundred miles out of an existing sixteen hundred miles, when these lines are built, and out of, possibly, 3,000 miles, when their branches and extensions in all directions are built. To take power under this clause to acquire (500 or 700 miles would not be a useful power, nor one of which it would be proper in future for us to avail ourselves. If we were submitting, to parliament a general scheme of assistance to a completed line from one side of the continent to the other, we might consider the advisability of stipulating that the government should at any time avail itself at its option of taking that property over. But the same reason does not apply, it appears to me, to the case of a few miles of Mr. BROCK.
railway such as we are now dealing with. In making this remark I do not profess to indicate what would be the conclusion at which my colleagues would arrive. I propose to ask the committee to rise, when this last section is passed, and ask leave to sit again, in order to dispose of one sectiou which has been left standing. I may say to the hon. gentleman that I will take this subject up with my colleagues in the meantime. But I may intimate to him. what strikes me at the moment, that it is not likely to meet with approval,.
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: There is a strong feeling in our part of the country that something of this kind should be done. There is a possibility that we may have to acquire all the roads in the country, and when we are giving a large amount of aid to an undertaking of this kind, it is only right that provision should be put in the Bill whereby the government may take over the road if they see fit. If that time never arrives, the power will never be exercised, but it is just as well to have the power.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: It should be distinctly understock that the power should only be exercised in case of a national road from the Atlantic to the Pacific, not merely a small portion of a transcontinental road. If at any time the government should make up their minds to aid a transcontinental road, or to acquire various roads that together would make a continuous road to the Pacific, this might be a useful power. But the government of Canada should not take power to spend the money of Canada to acquire a portion of a railroad, a railroad in Manitoba for instance, it should be a national road of a national character.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I want to point out to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals that I think the words ' Governor in Council' at the end of section 8 should perhaps be stricken out and that the words which appear at the commencement of section 7 should be substituted. Does the hon. gentleman follow what I mean ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Strike out the words * Governor in Council ' and substitute the words ' any authority created by parliament for that purpose.' Is the idea really to leave that matter to the discretion of parliament ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: I think this would be supplementary. Would that not be the view of the hon. gentleman ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext: Supplementary to what ?

subtopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES.
speechtext:
Supplementary to the power of revision, or to the consent of the Railway

Committee of the Privy Council, or of the railway commission. X do not think it would repeal or rescind the application of the Railway Act in any way. This is more in the nature of a contractual arrangement. It does not alter the Railway Act in any respect. I think it would simply mean that the supervision and authority of parliament which might be exercised over the railway might be exercised by the Governor in Council in the manner mentioned here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.

speechtext:
House proceeded to consider amendments by the Senate to Bill (No. 17) to aid in the
settlement of railway labour disputes.-The Postmaster General.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: What are the amendments ?

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: Section 6 of the Bill has been amended by the Senate by striking out the words ' not exceeding ten days,' and inserting in lieu thereof * within such time as the minister may fix.' Section 6 is a section providing for filling vacancies on the conciliation committee. There is no objection to that amendment. I move that the amendment be concurred in. In section 7, fourth line, the Senate suggests the insertion of the words ' and the Prince Edward Island Railway.' The government also concur in that amendment. In the original section 7 the Prince Edward Island Railway was treated as part of the Intercolonial Railway, but it has always been treated in our accounts under a separate head, and the amendment of the Senate is to make it clear that the Prince Edward Island Railway will be in the same position as the Intercolonial Railway.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: Which lieutenant governor would be selected then.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext:
If the dispute were in Prince Edward Island it would be proper that the lieutenant governor of that province would choose. The original section fourteen provided that witnesses might be summoned by the board to give evidence, and the Senate amendment makes it that the chairman of the board shall have power. I propose to move that the following answer be 'sent to the Senate :
That this amendment be amended by striking the words ' the chairman of ' for the reason that it is Inexpedient to leave it in the discretion of any one member of the board to determine who should be summoned as a witness, but the question should be determined by the board or the majority thereof.
In section fourteen also, the Senate declare that witnesses shall be entitled to their witness fees, whereas the original section does not give us a legal right to fees. It has been pointed out to me by the representatives of the railway employees that in many instances they are paid by their unions or by the men for taking an interest in these matters, and they do not wish to have it made possible that the men should get double pay for attending as witnesses. They think that such a thing might not expedite proceedings, and the men themselves have requested that they be not put in that position.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: I think it better that the men should be paid by the country than that they should be paid by one of the parties to the suit in whose interest they are appearing.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext:
Under the original Bill it is quite in order for the board to use its discretion in the matter. In a parliamentary committee for instance a witness has no right to his witness fees unless the committee says he should be paid them, and the same principle can be applied here. I move :
That the fourth amendment be disagreed to for the following reason : Because many of the witnesses may be' properly remunerated for their attendance as witnesses other than by payment by the board, and it would be inexpedient to make it possible for witnesses to be over remunerated for their attendance as witnesses ; and therefore it is more in the public interest that it be in the discretion of the board to determine in what cases persons should be paid for,their attendance as witnesses.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: In what section is that discretion conferred on the board.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: It is not necessary to confer by express language upon the board the right to recommend. The board would have that right of recommendation, and under clause twenty-four if it were necessary to do so, the Minister of Labour might pass the necessary regulations applying to such a subject.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext:
I would be inclined to differ from my hon. friend with - regard to that. This board is the creature of a statute and has no implied powers outside of the four corners of that statute.
The TOSTMAjSTER .GENERAL. Section twenty-four would give that power to the minister.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: I have a great deal of doubt that such would be the case. I would not agree with the Postmaster General unless he would contend that section twenty-four is wide enough to allow him to practically construct a new Act out of this. That section confers upon the minister power to make certain regulations, but I do not think that it gives him power to provide for the payment of money.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: That money would have to be voted by parliament and the vote would determine how it would be applied. The board would, under that authority, have the power to pay witnesses if there was a vote for that purpose.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: It might be covered by the vote of parliament, but I do not think it would come under section twenty-four.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: If under the Bill as it stands the board could allow witness fees, they could also allow counsel fees and solicitors costs under section eighteen.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext:
Exactly.
Amendments read the second time.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL moved that the first, second, and fifth amendments be agreed to.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext:
That the third amendment of the Senate to the said Bill be amended by leaving out the words ' the chairman of ' in the said amendment, because it is inexpedient to leave it in the discretion of any one member of the board to determine who may be summoned as witnesses, but the question should be determined by the beard or a majority thereof.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax), in the usual course, in any legal proceeding-and this is to all intents and purposes a legal proceeding-either parly has the right to summon any witness he sees fit. It is an everyday procedure to go to the registrar or clerk of the court and get a subpoena for any witness you require, and it would hardly appear to me that the amendment proposed by the Senate Is an unreasonable one. It would rather seem to be with a view of convenience. Otherwise you must have the formal meeting of the board before either party shall have the right to subpoena a witness. It seems to me you add a good deal of red tape to the procedure of the committee when you decline to adopt the amendment which the Senate has sent down to us. Particularly is that the case, in view of the fact that by the further amendment which is suggested, witnesses are to go without any witness fees. If they are to do that, it would hardly seem necessary to call three members of the board to authorize a witness to be summoned.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OR RAILWAY LABOUR DISPUTES.
speechtext: The amendment of the Senate is not adding to the convenience of the machinery, but rather putting an additional block upon it, taking from a majority of the board and vesting in the chairman alone the right to say who shall and who shall not be summoned. Practically it would be left in his hands in most cases, but it is not advisable to exclude the jurisdiction of the other two. The board in the first place would have to meet to organize and choose their umpire. So that I do not think in the practical working of it out, any trouble would arise from this power being given to the majority of the board.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: MONTREAL HARBOUR COMMISSIONERS.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved third reading of Bill (No. 201) to provide for further advances to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal. He said :	In moving the third reading of

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock) moved second reading of Bill (No. 208) to amend the Post Office Act.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman would be good enough to explain the Bill.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: So much of the Bill is in detail that it would perhaps be better understood if it were taken up clause by clause in committee. The first section deals with railway mail clerks, and it alters their status. Under the law at present in force and which has been in force for many years, third-class railway mail clerks are paid, on appointment $480 ; after two years service, $520 ; after five years, $560 ; after ten years, $640; In the second class they are paid on appointment, $600 ; after two years, $640 ; after five years, $720 ; after ten years $800. First class clerks are paid on appointment $720 ; after two years, $800 ; after five years $880 : after ten years, $960, which is the maximum. In addition to these payments, they also receive what is called mileage, being half a cent of train run during certain hours, and one cent a mile during certain other hours. It happens that under the existing law the increase of salary of a railway mail clJrk is very slow, and his promotion from class to class is equally slow, and depends, not wholly on length of service or efficiency, but also on the chance of there being a vacancy above him. Under the Bill I am introducing it is proposed to give all railway mail clerks who are deserving annual increases, abolishing classes. They will enter the probationary period of six months at $400 a year. The pay for the probationary period to-day is I believe, at $300 a year. After a mail clerk has been in the service not more than six months probationary period and has shown capacity and is likely to be deserving of apodntment, he will be confirmed in his appointment. He then receives $500 a year and thereafter an annual increase of $30 until he attains a maximum of $1,200 a year, in addition to which he receives mileage. That is to say, a railway clerk will have a minimum salary of $500 a year and a maximum salary of $1,200 a year, together with mileage.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: You abolish the classes?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Y'es, so that they all may get their annual increase and reach the maximum. This maximum is $240 more than it was under the old Act. The railway clerks calling is a very hazardous and labourous one. He has to run many risks and is frequently the victim of a railway accident, in which he very often receives injury and sometimes loses his life. Parliament has on several occasions in the last few years given a compassionate allowance to the widows and orphans of railway mail clerks where deaths have ensued. It happens not unfrequently that mail clerks are in accidents from which they appear to emerge with safety, but which nevertheless make them the victims later on of nervous diseases which shorten their lives. I think $1,200 is not unreasonable. The mileage varies, depending on the run. It is not quite possible to give an estimate, but I think it would amount, on an average, to $300 or $400 a year, but it is not all clear gain. When a man is travelling, even officially, on a railway car, he is put to more expense than if he were living in his own home.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Does the hon. the minister intend to increase the salaries of first class railway mail clerks who are now in receipt of the maximum ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
They will get an increase at the rate of $50 a year up to $1,200.
Mr. LEMIEUX, What is the maximum now ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: $900, but only a small proportion can obtain the maximum. Many are detained in the third class where the maximum is $640. The majority of mail clerks' to-day are not receiving more than $800. As there seems to be a disposition to go into details, perhaps we had better go into committee.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman want to get out of committee tonight ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I am iu no hurry.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax), We expected to have the Railway Commission Bill.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I shall leave the Bill in committee after we make some progress.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not want it to be understood that we will go out of committee to-night.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon.
On section 1, subsection (a)-railway mail clerks, appointment and salary.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Are we to understand that this provision is to apply only to persons who are hereafter appoiuted ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No, the hon. gentleman will see by subsection (f) that it applies to the present clerks.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Take the case of a clerk who is getting the maximum of $960 under the present law, will he be given $1,200 at once ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No, the Bill provides that he will be eligible for au increase of $50 each year until the maximum of $1,200 is reached, but no increase shall be granted, except in the case of a railway mail clerk over sixty years of age, unless the clerk, within a period of twelve months, passes a satisfactory case examination.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: In other departments of the service, I understand that the maximum of a first class clerk is $1,500.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There are different salaries for different classes of first class clerks. The salaries are not the same for the inside and the outside service. I am only now dealing with tin) railway mail clerks.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I understand that, but I am within my right when I refer to these other officials in the hon. gentleman's department. As I understand it, wheh you come to make up the superannuation, it is made up from the salaries and not from the mileage allowance. Is that not true ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is on the fixed salary.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The reason the railway mail clerks do not receive as high a maximum as the clerks in the service is that their salary is augmented by the mileage. This mileage is not taken into account in making up the superannuation, so that the railway mail clerk who has reached the maximum receives considerably less than a first class clerk who receives $1,500-and those who have not reached the maximum, proportionately still less. This seems to me an unjust discrimination against the railway mail clerks. Their service, as the hon. minister lias stated, is very hazardous, they are exposed to much greater risks than those safely seated in their offices. If there is to be any discrimination, it seems to me, in all justice and fair play, it should be in favour of the railway mail clerks. You could take into account a railway mail clerk's mileage for three, four or five years preceding superannuation. There must be some record of how that mileage is paid. My hon. friend from Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) shakes his head. It seems to me it would be a very easy matter to strike an average for the years preceding in counting the superannuation of the railway mail clerks. I wish to call the special attention of the minister to this matter. As he has introduced a Bill to increase the salaries of these officials -and very properly, because I believe that the salaries of most of the civil servants of this country should be increased, for they were fixed many years ago, when the cost of living was nothing like what it is at the present time, and I believe there should be a readjustment all round-it seems to me he should take advantage of the present occasion and remove an unjust discrimination against the railway mail clerks in this matter.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I am sorry that this Bill does not extend much further than it does. There are the letter carriers in the different cities who are just like beasts of burden, carrying large mails in all weathers, and sometimes having to take a hand-cart to carry the postal matter they must deliver. Another class that should be considered are the clerks in the inside service, who work night and day at very small salaries. If you deal with one part of the service, you should take a wider view and deal with the whole service. If we have surplus funds, as the hon. Minister of Finance has informed us that we have, there is no way in the world in which our money can be so wisely and so justly spent as in improving the position of the civil service of the Dominion.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Ross) has evidently not read the Bill, for it deals with a large number of the post office officials, including the letter carriers.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What clause ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is in the Bill, and we shall reach the clause in due course.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Could the minister tell what is the mileage allowance on the average for the railway mail clerk ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I could not say exactly, but it would average $300 or $100.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I desired the information for the benefit of my hon. friend from King's, N.B. (Mr. Fowler), who thinks the superannuation of railway mail clerks is not sufficient. He must remember that at appointment they get wages largely in excess of the ordinary clerk going into the department. The ordinary clerk entering the service receives $400, but the railway mail clerk commences with $400 and mileage of, perhaps, $400.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: But that does not help them very much when it comes to the time for superannuation, which may be twenty-five or thirty years afterwards, when he has got ail this money expended. This superannuation allowance is for the comforts of his declining years, when he has worn himself out in the service of the country. I do not know whether any representations have or have not been made to the minister by the railway mail clerks ; but I have been requested to bring this matter before the committee when the Bill was before the committee, and I have done so. I think it is a ease that requires fair treatment, and, at present, the railway mail clerks are discriminated against.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The reason why I shook my head when the hon. member (Mr. Fowler) was making a statement was not that I did not wish to see the railway mail clerks receive a larger superannuation allowance, but what struck me at the time was that you must base this superannuation on some fixed sum.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: For the reason that the amount earned in mileage may be different every year. It is different every year with a different class.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Well !

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: One railway mail clerk may have a run on which he will make a good deal more than another will make on his run.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why can you not strike an average ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why should you strike an average ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why not ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Suppose you have two railway mail clerks, one putting in more
time than the other and travelling more. Why should his time be averaged up to help out one who does not do so much ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: You do not need to strike an average as between two railway mail clerks, but strike an average for each railway mail clerk, mileage for two, three or five years preceding the time of his superannuation. Treat him irrespective of everybody else, and you will find that it will practically average about the same.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: If it could be worked out, I should certainly be willing that it should toe done. I quite agree with what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) says upon tlie subject generally, but it struck me that there was this difficulty in the way, and that is why I shook my head.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Suppose you were superannuating a railway mail clerk. You take the average mileage he had made for the five years preceding superannuation and base your calculations upon that. Suppose he has earned an average of $300 a year for five years. If you have a clerk who is receiving $1,200 of salary, the maximum amount, you get $1,500 on which to base his superannuation allowance.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I would be inclined to agree with the hon. member if it could be worked out.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There is another point to be remembered in this superannuation question. If these gentlemen do not receive a superannuation based upon their mileage they are not taxed upon their mileage. Deductions are only made from salaries, and superannuations are based upon salaries from which deductions are made. If the railway mail clerks were to be superannuated on a higher basis, of course these extra payments would have to be treated as additions to salaries, and deductions made accordingly.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That is quite reasonable, of course.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: At all events, the whole question of superannuation is one for consideration in a superannuation Act. This Bill does not deal with superannuations at all, there is a civil service Superannuation Act that deals with this matter. It would not be proper in a Bill of this kind to deal with superannuations.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I beg to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to another matter in connection with the mail service, and that is the country postmasters.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Would not that come up more conveniently on the estimates. ? There ate many interesting subjects connected with the post office, and that is one of them, but it is hardly germane to the question of railway mail clerks.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Nevertheless, perhaps the minister will pardon me for a' minute. I know there are a number of small postmasters in my county, and I am sure there are many in other counties similarly situated, who are receiving very small amounts indeed. They are supposed to be in their offices from morning until night, compelled sometimes to remain until ten or eleven o'clock waiting for some persons to come in for their mail matter. Why, the cost of the oil they burn is more than the amount they receive from the government. When the Postmaster General is making his provisions for the railway mail clerks, I think he might well consider the country postmasters and the small amount they receive at the present time.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think the Postmaster General is doing tardy justice to one of the most useful class of officers in the public service. The increase he is giving them is not at all too much, indeed I think the House would endorse his action in making the increase still greater. There is a good deal in what has been said by the hon. member for King's (Mr. Fowler) respecting the superannuation allowance that should be given to these men when they retire from the public service. I would also like to suggest to the Postmaster General the advisability "of providing some scheme of insurance for these men. He has drawn attention to the fact that in many instances accidents have occurred to these men while in the discharge of duty by which they have been incapacitated. A reasonable provision in the form of an accident insurance would be a very valuable protection to them. I brought this matter up two or three years ago, and I would like to ask the minister if he has given the subject consideration. These are a most deserving body of public officials, and worthy of his special attention.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I have thought of a good many things in connection with the railway mail service, some of which I have disposed of. I have been for a long time contemplating some provision by which the government should decree by statute the payment of a bonus, or a compassionate allowance to the family of a railway mail clerk losing his life in the service, or to himself in case of accident. I am not aware that parliament has ever paid a compassionate allowance to the family of a railway mail clerk who has lost his life in the service, until the present government invited parliament to do so, when parliament unanimously agreed to the proposition. It has been our policy ever since coming into power to give a compassionate allowance of $2,000, a fixed sum, to the dependents of a railway mail clerk who has lost his life in the service. But we have not deemed it wise to put that policy into an Act of parliament for this reason :	A

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: railway mail clerk may or may not have a cause of action against the company in case, of accident, or his family a cause of action against the company in case of his death. So that if by law he was entitled to a certain indemnity from the government, that fact would doubtless be taken into consideration in any suit against the railway company for damages. Therefore, it has been deemed wiser to leave the matter in the discretion of the government to deal with each case as it comes up. In the case of an accident to a railway mail clerk in the service, the invariable practice has been to allow him his full pay while incapacitated, and I recall one clerk receiving pay for several years, having been injured in an accident. That practice of giving an indemnity has worked well. I do not think any government would treat such cases otherwise than generously, so I think we had better leave that matter as it stands at present.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I made the proposition of an accident insurance as a matter of business, so that all the railway mail clerks in the service might be assured of securing a reasonable sum in case of accident. If he lost his life his dependents would be entitled to a fixed sum. In that way these men would be reasonably sure of the protection to themselves and their families to which they are entitled in view of the arduous character of the employment in which they are engaged. I would suggest that they contribute annually a small sum as part of the premium, so that $2,000 or $3,000 might be paid to them in case of accident.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Practically, without taxing them at all, we have adopted a system of giving a gratuity to their dependents in case of loss of life. That is an insurance without any assessment. If he desires any additional insurance, he can easily get it, considering that he is not obliged to contribute anything to the gratuity of $2,000 which we have been giving.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What about accidents where he may not lose his life.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We carry them on with full pay.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There is another matter to which I wish to draw the attention of the minister, and bring up now instead of waiting for the estimates, when I may not be present. I hold in my hand an envelope marked ' form No. two, instructions to masters of vessels arriving from foreign ports.' These instructions read as follows -
By the Act of Congress approved March 2, 1S95. on and after July 1, 1895, you are required. immediately upon landing, and before entering your vessel at the custom house, to mail to the auditor for the treasury depart-

ment, Washington, a true copy of the manifest of your vessel.
Then, on another part of the envelope, it says :
Collectors of customs and boarding officers will supply masters of vessels with these envelopes, and instruct them in the requirements of the law.
Further it says :
Any master using this envelope to mail manifest will not be required to pay postage.
That has been the law heretofore, but this year the officials of the American government, when they furnish these envelopes, insist upon postage being paid.
Instructions to American customs officials insist upon payment of postage.
Whenever the captain of a Canadian vessel entering a United States port, mails a manifest to Washington as required by law, he is obliged to pay postage. If any American coming into Canada is required to send a document to the Minister of Customs otto any department of the government, the document comes postage free. Postmaster General ought to look into immediately because captains of vessels find it very inconve'u-ient every time they go into a United States port as in the case of ferries running to the United States four or five times a day, when mailing a manifest to be obliged to pay postage. subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Is it the intention of the Postmaster General to continue this yearly case examination in the case of a man vyho has been ten, twenty or thirty years in the service ? I find in subsection (h) of this section that :
The railway mail clerks over sixty years of age shall not be required to pass the case examination.
Surely, after a man has been in the service fifteen or twenty years he should not be obliged to continue the case examination until he is sixty years of age. I think if the hon. minister provided that after a man had been twenty years in the service he should not be required to pass the case examination it would work better than making a limit of sixty years of age as is done iu subsection (h). I make that suggestion.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I suppose the hon. gentleman is familiar with the nature of the case examination ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Railway mail clerks will often continue on the same run for a long term of years, but they are liable to be shifted from place to place and if a man were shifted it would be most essential that he should understand the case examination for the route to which he has been transferred. Notwithstanding that there are constant changes in the running of trains and stage routes, the establishment of additional offices and so on, and it is necessary for a man to keep up with the case work. It is. as necessary for him to know his case examination next year as it is this as there are so many changes in routes.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I make the suggestion because of the. provision in subsection (h) which says that at sixty the case examination should stop. Why, if it is necessary, that a man should keep up his case work, should he stop at sixty ? Are they sup erannuated then ? I would suppose that



when a railway mail clerk lias been in the service for twenty years and has passed the yearly case examination that you might drop it then.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: At the age of sixty years a railway mail clerk is given a latitude that perhaps is not given to him in earlier life. During the earlier period of his life he is getting his increase of !>50 a year. It is right, as his salary is increased that he should pass his case examination showing that he was deserving of it. If we did not have this case examination men might claim their increases and not give good service. It is of the greatest importance that railway mail clerks should understand their case work. It means that they shall understand as they are sorting the mails on the trains as they go at the rate of thirty or forty miles an hour what bags to put the letters in and what stations to put them off at. Bags are put on containing letters and correspondence for a great many different places. The railway mail clerk must Open a mail bag when he receives it on the train and distribute the contents into various other bags and see that this mail matter goes to its proper destination. If he does not do so, if he is not familiar with the case work, he will put the mail matter into the wrong bags and the letters will be misdelivered.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is just possible that this case examination may work out a hardship in case a man were sent to a different route than that upon which he had been running immediately before the case examination was held. Because of this arbitrary provision in subsection (li) the examination would cease at the age of sixty. I think if a man has been in the service for twenty years he should be relieved from a further annual examination. However, if the Postmaster General insists that this is a better plan we must defer to his judgment.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: If a railway mail clerk passes his examinations regularly for five years, why would it not be sufficient to provide that he shall only be required to pass his examination upon a ehange of route.

speechtext: There are changes every year in connection with every route.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
If a man continues on one road for a long time and he becomes quite familiar with the offices, he may be put to great disadvantage if he is changed several times in a year.

speechtext: Is there any time limit under the present law when they get promotion ?

speechtext: No.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is a matter of discretion with the minister.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: When a vacancy happens by death or otherwise.

speechtext: Then a man would have to wait until another was removed to a higher sphere.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Something like that.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There does not seem to be a limit of time as to when the notice shall he given. He can wait a year or two and then come in.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I let him take advantage of all the benefits he can get out of the old Act and out of this Act.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: In connection with subsection ' g,' I would like to ask the lion. Postmaster General a question. I take it that persons coming under the provisions of the Act would start at their present salary, whatever that may be, and that time already served would not count upon the subsequent increase of $50. speechtext: A man may not have received an increase for years.

speechtext: Do you propose to give him $50 for each year that Re has been without an ipcrease ?

speechtext: I should think that would be a fair interpretation of it.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Does the hon. Postmaster General propose, in the case of a man who has been three or four years without an increase, that he shall receive three or four times the $50 ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No, I do not propose that. I propose just what the Bill says, that if a railway mail clerk has not had an increase for a year or longer, he becomes eligible for an increase. If when this Act comes into force a man has not had an increase for a year, he would be eligible for an increase at once.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Then we are to understand that all the railway mail clerks will get increases under the provisions of this Act if they have not received an increase within a year before the 1st of July ?

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: They will be eligible for an increase at the expiration of one year from the date when they received the last increase.	-

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: And the case examination will have nothing to do with that increase ?

speechtext:
I do not say that. They have to pass the case examination. The increases do not all date from the 1st of July. Suppose a man had an increase six months ago, he would not get another increase until six months from now. I think the case examination is held in the fall of the year, and any man who passed the case examination last fall would be entitled to an increase without having to pass another case examination within the year.

speechtext: If the men are thoroughly qualified, would it not be a hardship, after doing this tardy justice, to retain this $50 for six or twelve months from now V Because I understand from what the hon. gentleman says that they are not entitled to the statutory increase of $50 unless they first pass the examination.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman understands the Bill. He complains of tardy justice. That has been passed by all the clerks of the current year.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: But unless they signify their desire to come under this Act, they cannot count their time until that is done.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: And I gather that they must pass the examination afterwards before they can get an increase. The Bill so reads.

speechtext:
Look at
subsection ' b ' of section 1.

speechtext: The Bill says ' unless the clerk within a period of twelve months passes a satisfactory case examination.' If you said ' has passed,' it would have a different meaning perhaps. Where do you date the period of twelve months from 7

This seems to me an opportune time to call the attention of the hon. the Postmaster General to a request that has been made to me. During that time the mail clerk is there and he has to get Mr. SPROULE.
I his meals and pay for them. He receives no extra remuneration or mileage, and yet he is on service during those hours, and I have been asked to put his case before the Postmaster General in order that an allowance may be made to him of twenty-five cents an hour or whatever sum might be deemed fair to be allowed for detentions of that nature.	.

speechtext:
