Section 4 of chapter 28 of the statutes of 1902 is amended by striking out the word ' six ' in the second line and substituting therefor the word ' three,' and by inserting in the eleventh line after the words ' responsible nature ' the words ' or in recognition of special efficiency and good conduct.'

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: This has to do with letter carriers. It is provided in the Act that the letter carriers serve a probationary period of six months during which they are in grade A. This cuts down the first probationary period from six to three months.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That only helps the new comers.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The section of the Act of 1902 provided that the letter carriers who were doing work of a specially responsible and onerous character might be put in grade E, which means a daily pay of $2.25. This amendment enables us to put into class, not only men performing duties of a special class, but also letter carriers who have shown especial efficiency and good conduct. Under the existing Act the promotion to grade E depends upon the nature of the work performed. If the letter carrier were serving a bank or were on some route that was especially laborious, he could be promoted. But, under this clause, a letter carrier who has a good record, without regard to the duties of his present route, can be put into grade E. Under this law a man could be promoted to grade E because of his past services.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Would it not be a graceful act upon the part of the minister to put all the letter carriers who are now in grade D into grade E where they could receive $2.25 a day instead of $2 a day ? The memorials and petitions and representations sent to the Postmaster General have been numerous:	These men are a verj- efficient
body of public servants and are a very poorly paid class.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: They are much better paid than when I took office.

I am not aware that that is the case. The hon. minister is making amendments affecting those appointed sinoe lie came into office, but he has left those in office when he came in exactly where they were.
No. no.

These men are now receiving $2 a day and the hon. minister is proposing, under this section, to widen the scope of the law, so that, if they can get the recommendation of the local superintendent they may be increased from $2 to $2.25 per day. It would be a graceful act for the Postmaster General, in view of the circumstances presented to him, increase of cost of living since he came into office, and so on, to give these men this pittance of 25 cents a day more. These men have appealed again and again to the Postmaster General. They will be satisfied with this increase, I am sure, and would redouble their diligence if that were possible to give a more efficient service. After all the extent to which the exchequer of the country would be affected would be very small, and this is a faithful body of public servants. As the hon. minister is widening the conditions under which they may receive this extra quarter of a dollar a day he should give it to all those who have reached the grade D.

I wish my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) had pleaded as eloquently in years gone by for these officials. He had an opportunity years ago to render a service to these people; but he makes his appeal only at this tardy day, when he sees that justice is being done there. As he speaks of letter carriers, 1 think I may say that I am quite as sympathetic as my hon. friend, and I think I am proving that in a practical way. Let me show, for the information of the committee, what is the present remuneration of the letter carriers. Under the Act we passed last session the letter carriers not in grade E could receive a maximum of $2 a day. As soon as this Bill goes through, every letter carrier who has a good record-and none others should be entitled to special consideration-may receive $2.25 a day. He will be in receipt, at that time' of the following sums :	For
313 days-although he has two weeks leave of absence, he is paid for full 313 working days-$626. There is also a provision in the Act of last session giving an extra reward to a letter carrier who has rendered good service during the year, of ten days extra holidays or, at his option $20. The letter carrier could therefore receive $2 for every working day, and also a $20 bonus or $046. Besides his two weeks holidays lie has the ordinary holidays observed throughout the country or portions of it. Also he is allowed uniforms, winter and summer of various kinds, which would mean
a saving to a letter carrier of about $50 a year. This would make $696. If the letter carrier gets his *extra 25 cents per day which the Bill contemplates, that would mean $78 making a total of>
$774 a year. And tlieir services, do not, I think exceed eight hours per day. My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) shakes his head. But I know what I am saying; they do not average more than eight hours a day. There is no necessity for my hon. friend to challenge the accuracy of that statement. I have it from the officials. And in many instances, their hours do not amount to anything like eight hours a day. Now, $774 is not bad pay for a letter carrier. I do not think that amount is realised, year in and year out, by many of the working people who, in one form or another, contribute to make up the pay of the letter carriers. At all events, whether more or less than workingmen, it is a great deal more than the letter carriers have heretofore obtained. Deducting the $50 for uniforms, it means practically $100 increase on a salary of $600.

Will the hon. Postmaster General please figure it out how the rate of those who reach the maximum cla'ss has been increased by $100 per year ? How many weeks' holidays did the men get prior to the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Wm. Mu-lock) coming into office ?
Three weeks.
That has been cut down to two weeks-away goes $14.

I do not understand the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Clarke's) reasoning under the old law they could get $600 and no more. Under this law they get more than I had first calculated. I said they received $100 more than under the old law, but they get $626 in wages and $20 bonus and $78 of increased pay under this clause, making a total of $724-practically an increase of $125 a year on a salary of $600. I think the letter carriers will be of the opinion that this is a substantial increase.
Did they get uniforms before the hon. gentleman came into office ?
I am not counting that in the comparative statement.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the letter carriers' position has improved by $125 since he came into office.
I say that under this Bill the letter carrier who gets the benefit of this Bill will have improved his pay by $124.	.
May I ask the hon. minister how many letter carriers in all the divisions of Canada earned $646 in salary last year ?
I do not think the application of the law has been in force a year yet.
But the law the hon. gentleman sp&ke about gave them $2 a day that is $626-
And the bonus.
A bonus of $20-that is 10 days at $2 a day. May I ask the Postmaster General how many men in any city of Canada earned $640 last year ?

I have explained to the hon. gentleman that the Act was only passed last year. The hon. gentleman himself was a party to having an option of six months granted them in which to elect to come in. It was left optional with the letter carriers to come in or remain out; some came in and some did not. Those that came in will get the benefit of this Act. I think when the time has arrived it will appear that they have gained a good deal more under the new law than they would under the old.
How many postmen have come in under the new Act ?
I am not able to say.
Will the hon. gentleman say that six men in the Toronto division have come in under the new Act ?
Yes ; more than six.
More than six who have reached the maximum of $600 a year before the new Act was passed ?
I think so.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will get the information before the committee reports the Bill, and also as concerns Montreal.
I will get the information, and keep the Bill in committee for another sitting.
Is it not a fact that those who came in under the provisions of the Act passed last year, lose all their pay in case of sickness ?
Yes.
Was that the case under the old law ?
The hon. gentleman is familiar with both the old law and the new.

I would like to know how many men, who were receiving $600 a year when the new law came into force, have Mr. CLARKE.
taken advantage of it in each division of the postal service.

I will get the information for the hon. gentleman.
Mi-. KEMP. How many years does a letter carrier have to remain in the service before he reaches the maximum ?
Under the old law, between eight and nine years ; under the Act of last session, he can attain the maximum in a little over four years.
I think this is perhaps an opportune time to bring again to the attention of the minister the very small allowances made to country postmasters.
That has been up two or three times.

So has the question of giving an increased duty on vegetables. I am not aware that the hon. gentleman ever cast a vote in this House to assist the market gardeners or the postmasters throughout his riding. I have drawn the attention of the Postmaster General to that question, I dare say, two or three times ; I am not aware that the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) ever drew attention to it, or cared a button whether the postmasters in his riding got a salary at all or not.
You do not know what the member for West York has been doing.

No ; but we do know something that he did in his riding. What he has been doing behind the scenes, certainly we know not. But leaving that matter aside, I certainly think that while we are making such ample provision for the letter carriers in the city of Toronto for working eight hours a day-and I am not complaining of the amount they are receiving-I think some further provision should be made for country postmasters. It is a crying shame that throughout the rural districts men, and women too, nave to give their services practically for nothing, for sums ranging from $12 up to $30 and $40 a year. Yet in order that the public service may be carried on, people have to give their time voluntarily for these insignificant sums. It is true that in some sections of the country these small pittances are added to by the people themselves who receive mail matter, in order to maintain an office. That should not be the case. Whilst the letter carriers in the cities are being considered, I desire to make an appeal on behalf of the rural postmasters. There is no doubt that many of them are entirely underpaid, and I do not think the Postmaster General could do a better service, something for which he would receive more gratitude from the people, than by giving a better compensation to these men who are performing this service practically for nothing.

I desire to add one word to what has been said by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson). It seems to me this matter can well be considered by the Postmaster General, though I am aware that it would involve probably a considerable increase to the expenditure of the department. Still, it is not right that the country postmasters should be expected to attend to an office for the paltry sum of $12 per annum. There is a case in my own constituency where a daily mail runs through a district passing the post office in the morning and once again in the afternoon. That necessitates the postmaster's house being kept open, and-he or his wife must be there to attend to that mail, even though no mail is left or taken. Certainly some provision should be made for better remuneration for country postmasters, and I strongly urge their case upon the attention of the minister.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I must remind the Postmaster General of a deputation that came ail the way from Manitoba on this very subject. The postmasters in Manitoba are underpaid, and there is a strong feeling out there that something should be done in their favour. If my memory does not fail, I believe the Postmaster General promised these men that he would give their request his most favourable consideration. I do not know what that amounts to, I see nothing in this Bill to help them, and unless we get the promise of another Bill on this subject, I am afraid that our friends from Manitoba will have no occasion to thank the Postmaster General for the kind reception he gave them when they came here.

I would like to say in respect to what has just fallen from the lips of the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. La-Riviere) that very great complaint exists thoughout my own constituency and other constituencies similarly situated near Montreal in regard to the pay of country postmasters. They have, perhaps, not so much to do in the winter, but in summer all these places around Montreal are resorted to by the citizens of Montreal, and a very great increase of work falls upon the country postmasters, and I think it would be the duty of the department to give them some extra allowance for this. In pegard to the (juestion raised a moment ago by my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke), I would like to know if, when the hon. Postmaster General brings down the information in respect to the letter carriers and the salaries they have reached in the city of Toronto, he will be kind enough to do the same thing in regard to the letter carriers of the city of Montreal, because I have had the same Inquiry, I presume, from Montreal as my hon. friend has had from Toronto, so that we can advert to the question when we get the information from the hon. minister.
I understand that it does not require a statutory provision to increase the salaries of postmasters and that it is done by regulation ?
That is correct.

Then, it is not necessary to deal with it in connection with this Bill, but I would like to say a word in regard to what has been said about country postmasters.
